en: When about to pile the Gārhapatya fire, he sweeps it away with a Palāśa branch.
For in piling the Gārhapatya, he establishes it;
and whatever pilers of fire there have been, they are all established upon this very earth. Thus, when he sweeps it away, he sweeps away those who have already been established.
"Do not settle, do not occupy"—that is, "Go away, depart, and creep away. This means: "Go away, depart, and creep away from here. 7.1.1.[2] "Ya" (ya).
To those creeping things that are there, he says: "Ye who are here, ancient ones, and ye who are new ones"—that is to say, "ye who are here, eternal ones, and ye who are of the present time.
[7.1.1.3] "Yama has assigned you this end of the earth."
"Yama indeed rules over this resting place; he himself grants us this resting place in it.
"The fathers have made this world for us," [he says].

Yama is indeed the nobility (kṣatra) and the fathers are the common people (viś). When a nobleman, being in agreement with the common people, grants him a dwelling on this earth, that is a gift well-bestowed; and so Yama, the nobility, being in agreement with the common people and the fathers, grants him a dwelling on this earth. 7.1.1 [5]
He sweeps away with a *palāśa* branch.
The *palāśa* is indeed the Brahman; thus he sweeps away those things that have settled by means of the Brahman.
He does so with a mantra; the mantra is indeed the Brahman; thus he sweeps away those things that have settled by means of the Brahman. He throws it out toward the north. 7.1.1.[6]
Then he scatters saline soil.
The Gārhapatya is indeed this world, and saline soil is cattle; thus he places cattle in this world.
Therefore, these cattle are in this world. 7.1.1 [7]
Furthermore, as to why he scatters the *uṣas* (dust):
Prajāpati created offspring; he created them with different amniotic sacs (*ulba*), and they did not agree with one another.
He desired, "May they agree," so he made them have the same amniotic sac. He made the *uṣas* their common amniotic sac, and they agreed.
Therefore even now, those who share the same womb recognize one another. Indeed, he who sacrifices sacrifices with the thought, "May I have the same womb as the gods.
In that he scatters the *ūṣa* salt, he thereby comes to have the same womb as the gods.
"Thou art recognition," [he says].

For they recognized this as "the support of desires"; the saline soil (ūṣāḥ) are indeed cattle, and "the support of desires" means "may there be for me the support of desires from you," which is to say, "may there be cattle for me from you.
With these, he covers the entire Gārhapatya hearth; for the layering of the Gārhapatya is the womb, and the saline soil is the caul; thus, he covers the entire womb with the caul.
He covers it. Then he pours down sand.
Sand is indeed the ash of Agni Vaiśvānara; for this [fire-altar] is indeed Agni.
One is about to sacrifice with the Vaiśvānara [offering]. Indeed, fire does not burn its own ash excessively; [he does this] so that there may be no excessive burning.
Furthermore, as to why he scatters sand:
sand is the seed of Agni Vaiśvānara; for this Agni is indeed...
When one is about to perform the Vaiśvānara sacrifice, [he says]: "Nothing indeed is produced from that which is seedless; let there be production from this seed.
[He then addresses the earth with: "Thou art the ash of Agni; thou art the soil of Agni."
The ashes of the fire are exhausted, while the sand-grains are unexhausted; he thus makes this [altar] unexhausted. With them he covers the entire Gārhapatya hearth.
The Gārhapatya altar is indeed the womb, and the sand-grains are the seed; he thus places the seed in the entirety of the womb. 7.1.1. [12]
Then he encloses it with the enclosing-stones (*pariśrit*).
The enclosing-stones are indeed the womb; thus he encloses this emitted seed within the womb.
Therefore, the seed that is emitted is enclosed by the womb. 7.1.1 [13]
Furthermore, as to why he encloses it with the enclosing-stones (*pariśrit*):
the Gārhapatya is indeed this world, and the enclosing-stones are the waters;
he thus surrounds this world with water. He surrounds it on all sides with the ocean; therefore, [he surrounds] this world.
"The ocean flows around it on every side, turning to the right; therefore the ocean flows around this world, turning to the right.
By means of a trench, therefore the ocean flows around this world by means of a trench.
"Thou art piled," he says.
"For he piles them around," he says, for he indeed piles them around; "rest as piled upwards," he says while laying them down upwards;
therefore the ocean swells upwards. Now, if he were to lay them down sideways, the ocean would surely wash away this entire world at once. He does not settle them; they are unsettled.

"The waters, with the *sūdadohas* [verse], speak over [them]. (7.1.1.15) The *pariśrit* bricks are indeed the bones; the *sūdadohas* is the vital breath (*prāṇa*). Indeed, there is no vital breath within the bones, except by means of a single sacrificial formula (*yajus*).
He lays down many bricks, for water is a single form; and as to why there are many enclosing-stones (*pariśrit*), it is because water is manifold.
Indeed, those enclosing-stones are the womb.
The saline soil (ūṣa) is the womb, the sand is the seed; the enclosing stones (pariśrit) are on the outside, while the saline soil is inside.

For the womb is outside and the amnion (ulba) is inside. The saline soil is on the outside and the sand is inside; for the amnion is outside and the seed is inside. From these [elements], indeed, one being born is born; it is from these very elements that he thus causes him to be born. 7.1.1. [17]
Then he piles this [altar] from there; he thereby transforms this very seed that has been cast, for it is in the womb that the seed which is cast is transformed. 7.1.1 [18]
He lays down four bricks facing eastward:
two behind, crosswise, and two in front. That which are the four laid down facing eastward constitute the body; as to why there are four, it is because this body is fourfold. Now, as for those...

What were his two thighs behind become his two arms in front; where the self is, that indeed becomes the head. 7.1.1.[19] Now, he fashions this very [sacrificial animal] here with wings and a tail. For in whatever manner the seed is fashioned in the womb, in that same manner it is born. Since he fashions it here with wings and a tail, therefore it is so there [in the other world].
"He is born with wings and a tail. Indeed, although he possesses wings and a tail, people do not perceive him as one who actually has wings and a tail.
Therefore, they do not see the embryo in the womb according to its true form; then, there in the other world, they see it possessed of wings and a tail;
therefore, once born, they see the embryo according to its true form.
He lays down four bricks first.

For it is the self that first comes into being when one comes into being. Sitting to the south facing north, he lays down the first brick on the northern part; thus indeed this fire-altar of his becomes built up toward the self. 7.1.1 [22]

"This is that fire in which Indra placed the pressed Soma"— this Gārhapatya fire is indeed this world, and the pressed Soma is the waters; thus, in this world, Indra placed the waters within his belly, for "the belly" refers to the middle.

"A thousandfold prize, like a steed that wins the seven," for the thousandfold prize is indeed the waters; "having won it, you are praised, O Jātavedas"—this means, "being piled up, you are piled up, O Jātavedas.
"O Agni, what splendor of yours is in heaven... [7.1.1.23]

"The sun indeed is his splendor in heaven; on earth [is] this Agni"—this refers to the fire that is on earth. "In plants, in waters, sacrifice"—this he says of that very fire which is in plants and in waters. "By whom the wide mid-region was spread out"—that is Vāyu. "He who is brilliant, he who is radiant, the surging one, the beholder of men"—he is the Great One.

"Bhānu, Arṇava, Nṛcakṣas"—this refers to that. "O Agni, you go toward the flood of heaven"—the waters indeed are the flood of this heaven; he goes toward them with smoke, and [he goes] toward the gods.
"You have spoken, O ye gods who are worthy of praise"—the gods who are worthy of praise are indeed the vital breaths (*prāṇas*), for they impel all thoughts (*dhiyas*).
"Those which are beyond the radiant realm of the sun, and those which stand below it, the waters"—this radiant realm is indeed this world where the sun shines;
thus he speaks of both the waters that are beyond it and those that are below it. 7.1.1 [25]
"Purīṣyas agnayas" means "the fires pertaining to cattle.

"Prāvaṇebhiḥ sajoṣasaḥ" is a form belonging to the departure, for the Gārhapatya fire is indeed the departure of Agni. "Juṣantāṃ yajñamadruho 'namīvā iṣo mahīḥ" [means] "May they, free from malice and disease, enjoy the sacrifice and the great nourishments."
"May they, free from malice and hunger, enjoy the great offerings"—this is what is meant.
He lays them down separately;
he thereby bestows upon the self those various desires that exist within it. He settles them all at once; he thereby makes the self one.

He performs [the rite] with the *sūdadohas* verse; he recites over it. The *sūdadohas* is indeed the vital breath (*prāṇa*); by means of the vital breath, he thus makes this continuous and joins it together.
[27] Then, having gone around behind...

Sitting to the north, facing south, he places the southern one of the two western bricks with the verse: "O Agni, the *iḍā*—the boon of many wondrous deeds, the gain of cattle. The *iḍā* is indeed cattle; verily, he thus invokes this blessing for him regarding cattle. "He accomplishes the most constant invocation for the one who calls"—the one who calls is indeed the sacrificer; may it be ours.
"Sūnu, tanaya, vijāvā"—"sūnu" means offspring; "O Agni, may this benevolent disposition of yours be toward us"—with these words he invokes a blessing.
7.1.1.[28] Then the subsequent verse:
"This is your seasonal womb, from which born you shone forth"—this is your eternal, seasonal womb.
"Since you were born, you have shone forth"—knowing this, O Agni, ascend; "then increase our wealth"—as the sacrificial formula is, so is its significance. These two are his thighs.
He lays them down separately, settles them separately, and pronounces the *sūdadohas* verse over them separately;

for these two thighs are separate. There are two [of them], for these two thighs are two. He lays them down behind, for these two thighs are behind. They are joined together at the front, for these two thighs are joined together at the front. 7.1.1.[30]
Then, having gone around again by that same way, sitting to the south facing north, he places the northern of the two eastern bricks at the front with the formula:
"Thou art a layer; by that deity, in the manner of Aṅgiras, sit firm. Then the southern one with: "Thou art a surrounding layer; by that..."

"By the deity, may it sit firm like Aṅgiras"— these are his two arms. He lays them down separately, settles them separately, and pronounces the *sūdadohas* verse over them separately, for these two are separate.
There are two arms; for these two arms are in the front part [of the body]. He places them in the front, for these two arms are in the front.
They are joined at the tips, for these two arms are joined at the tips. He places them thus: "these," "these," "these"—that is from left to right (dakṣiṇāvṛt), for that is the way among the gods.
He lays down eight bricks.

The Gāyatrī has eight syllables, and Agni is of the nature of the Gāyatrī; as great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, so great he thus builds him up. Five times he settles them; Agni consists of five layers, and there are five seasons.
The seasons are the year, and the year is Agni; as great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, so much of him he thus builds up. He settles eight bricks five times; that makes thirteen.
Thirteen months are a year, and there are thirteen layers of earth (purīṣa) for the fire-altar; as great as Agni is, as great as his measure is.
So much does that become. 7.1.1.[33] Then he lays down the Lokampṛṇā brick; its significance is above it, [and there are] three.
The first three layers are Agni; as great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, so much of him he thus builds up.
There are ten subsequent layers; their connection is this: first two, then ten, then one—for in this manner they build the layer.
These amount to thirteen; the significance of that has been explained. 7.1.1 [34]
These two sets together amount to twenty-one.
There are twelve months, five seasons, these three worlds, and yonder sun is the twenty-first; he thus establishes yonder sun upon this fire. 7.1.1.[35]
There are indeed twenty-one enclosing stones:
twelve months, five seasons, these three worlds, and this Agni as the twenty-first from yonder; he thus establishes this Agni upon yonder sun.

Now, when he lays these down in this manner, he thereby establishes these two one upon the other; thus these two are established one upon the other. He brings these two together here as two twenty-onefold [sets], for it is here that both of them—the Āhavanīya and the Gārhapatya—become so. 7.1.1. [36]

Then he pours down the loose soil (*purīṣa*). Its significance is as follows: he brings it from the edge of the *cātvāla* pit; for this *cātvāla* is Agni, and thus this [soil] of his becomes truly related to Agni. It should be level with the rim; its significance has already been explained. 7.1.1 [37]
It is one fathom in measure;
for man is indeed one fathom in measure, and Prajāpati is man, and Agni is Prajāpati. Thus he makes its womb commensurate with his own self. It is circular, for it is indeed circular.

This world is indeed the womb; the Gārhapatya fire-altar is circular, for this world is indeed circular. 7.1.1 [38] Then he pours those two together; he thereby brings about concord between them: "Be of one mind, may you two agree. Together with you...

"O Agni, you whose essence is the soil, make our minds united in their vows; may you two be of one mind for us"—with these words he pacifies them both for the sake of non-injury, so that they may not harm each other.
He pours [the earth] together with four [verses].
Thus, by means of those four-footed animals, he bestows this name upon these two;
moreover, since cattle are indeed food, it is by means of food that he bestows this name upon them.
One should not look at her when she is empty.
"One should not look at an empty [vessel]," it is said; for if he were to look at an empty one, it would swallow him.
Then he pours sand into it;
for sand is the seed of Agni Vaiśvānara.
He thus pours that seed, Agni Vaiśvānara, into her; it should be level with her mouth, for the significance of that has already been explained. 7.1.1 [42].
Then he unyokes her, so that she may not be scorched;
for whatever is yoked and is not unyoked is scorched. This indeed...
"Endowed with this, she bore the seed; she brought forth this Agni here; then she takes up another. For the fire-pan is indeed a woman;
therefore, when a woman first gives birth to a child, she then takes up another.
"Like a mother her son, the earth [bears] the one who is of the soil. (7.1.1 [43])

"As a mother her son, so may the Earth [bear] the cattle-fostering [fire]"—this means "she has borne Agni in her own womb. "O you who have borne him"—this means "she has indeed borne him in her own womb. "May Prajāpati Viśvakarman, in harmony with all the gods and the seasons, release her"—the seasons are indeed the All-gods; thus he releases her by means of them.

In harmony with all the gods and the seasons, Prajāpati Viśvakarman releases her; he places her to the north of the fire at a distance of one cubit (aratni). The significance of this has been explained.
Then, he pours milk into it.

Verily, he places this seed, and then he places milk; for the fire-pan is indeed a woman, and therefore when a woman conceives seed, she then bears milk. The sand is below and the milk is above, for seed is below and milk is above; he pours it into the middle so that it may correspond to that.
One should place a human head.
Prajāpati created living beings;
having created the beings and having run the entire race, he fell apart.
From him, as he lay thus relaxed, the vital breath (*prāṇa*) departed from his center; then vigor departed from him. When that had departed, he fell down.
From him, having fallen, food flowed out. And the eye that rested upon him—food flowed out from that, and it did not remain here.
"Then, what indeed shall be our support?
7.1.2.[2] Those gods said, "There is no other support than this; [let us resort] to this very Father Prajāpati."
"Let us fashion him; he alone shall be our foundation.
They said to Agni, "Indeed, there is no other foundation than you; [place] this Father Prajāpati upon you."
"Let us prepare it; that itself shall be our support. [They asked: "What will come of that for me?

They said, "This Prajāpati is indeed food. Let us eat this food with you as our mouth; let this food be ours through you as our mouth. "So be it," they said. Therefore, the gods eat food with Agni as their mouth, whatever [food] it may be.
When they offer to the deity, they offer indeed into the fire, for the gods made fire their mouth when they prepared that food.
Now, that vital breath which departed from his center—that is this very wind which blows here; and then...
The vigor that departed from him became that sun; and the food that flowed from him became whatever food exists in the year.
The gods then placed him within the fire.

Then, as soon as it had been stirred, Agni ascended it; that very vital breath which had departed from its center returned to it and entered it, and they placed it within him. Then, whatever vigor had departed from it, they placed that within him as well.

Whatever food flowed from that, they placed it within him; having prepared all of it in its entirety, they raised it upwards. Those worlds which they raised up are these very worlds. Of that [body], this world alone is the foundation.
Now, the fire that is in this world is his downward breath;
then, the intermediate space is his self; and the wind that is in the intermediate space is that very breath which is in the self.
The sky is his head; the sun and moon are his two eyes; and that which rested upon the eye is...
Therefore the moon is more completely closed; for from it food indeed flowed forth.
7.1.2.[8] This is truly that foundation which the gods then established; even today it remains that very foundation. So.
Thus, moreover, he will become superior to this. That Prajāpati who fell apart is this very Agni who is now being built up; and as for this empty fire-pan (ukhā), it is that [same part].
Before the offering, he lies down just as Prajāpati did when his breath had departed, his vigor had departed, and his food had flowed away;
empty, he lay there—this is his form.
He offers it into the fire.

Just as the gods then turned him over, so now when Agni mounts this [fire-pan] while it has been turned over, that very breath which had departed from his center returns to him; he places it within him.
Then, as for why he carries it after having fastened the gold plate (rukma) upon it:
Whatever vigor departed from him, he places that back into him; and when he lays on the fuel-sticks, whatever food flowed away from him, he places that back into him.
He lays them on both in the evening and in the morning.
For food flowed forth from both that day and that night;
these [oblations] should be performed throughout the entire year, for that Prajāpati from whom they departed is the year; thus he places all this [food] within him, in this very whole [year].

"In that [place] where this [fire-altar] is, one should not do this; nor should one place this upon it. 'One should not even look at it until it has been carried for a year,' so said Vāmakakṣāyaṇa, lest he see this father Prajāpati being cut asunder. At the end of a year, he [placed it].
Having prepared everything in its entirety, he raises it upwards, just as the gods raised it there [in the beginning].
Of this [altar], this world is indeed the Gārhapatya;
and that fire which is on the Gārhapatya is that very fire which is in this world.

Now, that which is between the Āhavanīya and the Gārhapatya is the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*). That fire which is on the Āgnīdhrīya altar is the wind (*vāyu*) that is in the intermediate space; it is his [the body's] Āhavanīya. The Āhavanīya itself is the sky (*dyu*).
And that fire which is in the Āhavanīya is the sun and the moon; this is his very self (*ātman*). 7.1.2. [13]
His head indeed is the Āhavanīya fire.

Now, that fire which is in the Āhavanīya is this very vital breath (prāṇa) in the head; it belongs to him. And as for the fact that he has wings and a tail, it is because this vital breath in the head has wings and a tail—the eye being the head.

The right ear is the right wing; the left ear is the left wing; the breath is the central body; speech is the tail, the foundation. Since they remain established after having eaten food by means of speech through the breaths, therefore speech is the tail, the foundation. 7.1.2. [14]

Now, that which is between the Āhavanīya and the Gārhapatya is the self (*ātman*). Then, the fire on the Āgnīdhrīya altar is that vital breath (*prāṇa*) which is within the self; it is his foundation (*pratiṣṭhā*). And the Gārhapatya is his very foundation. Now, as for that [fire] which is in the Gārhapatya...
That Agni is his downward vital breath. 7.1.2.
[15] Some build it as a triple layer, saying, "These three downward vital breaths are indeed [the fires]. One should not do so; they [thus] exceed [the proper measure].
They chant the perfection of the twenty-onefold stoma, then the perfection of the *anuṣṭubh*, and then the perfection of the *bṛhatī*.
Those who do so [attain this], for these are indeed one single form: the womb itself, the very act of procreation—namely, that these vital breaths flow downward;
for when one voids urine or excrement, one is truly procreated thereby. 7.1.2. [16]
Now, therefore, follows the correspondence.

There are twenty-one bricks and nine formulas; that makes thirty. With the settling and the *sūdadohas* verses, it becomes thirty-two. The *anuṣṭubh* consists of thirty-two syllables; thus, this is an *anuṣṭubh*. 7.1.2. [17]
There are indeed twenty-one enclosing formulas;

the formula for the removal [of the earth] is the twenty-second; and there is the formula for the saline soil (ūṣa), the formula for the sand (sikatā), the formula for the loose earth (purīṣa), and the formula for the fourfold pouring together; he releases [the cord] with the fifth.

Then, by three [syllables], this becomes the thirty-two-syllable *anuṣṭubh*; this is that *anuṣṭubh*. Now, these two *yajus* formulas are indeed just the *anuṣṭubh*, for the *anuṣṭubh* is speech; thus, these two are the form of speech.
The divine and the human—both of these are high and low. These two [verses] are indeed these three *anuṣṭubh*s.
This Gārhapatya fire-altar is piled up; therefore, these three *anuṣṭubh*s are here.
For at that time all these worlds are indeed accomplished here;
then they carry another thirty-two-syllable *anuṣṭubh* to the Āhavanīya fire-altar. That Āhavanīya is the sky, and that is the head.
Then one [verse] remains here; that is the Gārhapatya fire-altar, that is the foundation, and that is this world. 7.1.2. [20]
Now, as for these two *yajus* formulas:

that which is between the Āhavanīya and the Gārhapatya is this intermediate space (*antarikṣa*), and that is the body (*ātman*). Since there are two of them, therefore that [space] between the Āhavanīya and the Gārhapatya is narrower.
And therefore, among these worlds, the intermediate world (antarikṣa-loka) is the lowest.
This very speech, divided threefold, is the *anuṣṭubh* meter;
this Agni, having become the vital breath (*prāṇa*), moves along with it in the Āhavanīya fire.
The fire on the Āhavanīya altar is that breath, and it is yonder sun; the fire on the Āgnīdhrīya altar is the diffused breath (vyāna), and it is this wind which blows here;
the fire on the Gārhapatya altar is the upward breath (udāna), and it is this fire which is in this world.
One who knows thus indeed prepares all speech, all breath, and the entire self. 7.1.2. [22]
This very [verse] is indeed the Bṛhatī.

For those two sets of thirty-two syllables, that makes thirty-two; then these two Yajus formulas make thirty-four; Agni himself is the thirty-fifth. The metre does not depart from one syllable, nor from two; he is that.
It consists of two syllables; thus it becomes thirty-six, for the *bṛhatī* consists of thirty-six syllables.
Indeed, this [altar], when built up, attains the state of the *bṛhatī*. For in whatever manner seed is infused into the womb, in that same manner is it born.
Therefore, because he makes this *bṛhatī* here, this [altar], when built up, attains the state of the *bṛhatī*. 7.1.2. [23]

Regarding this they say: "Since this world is the Gārhapatya, the intermediate space (antarikṣa) the Dhiṣṇyas, and the sky the Āhavanīya—and since the intermediate space is not separated from this world—then why, after piling the Gārhapatya, does one pile the Āhavanīya and then the Dhiṣṇyas? These two worlds were originally together; when they separated, that which was the space between them became the intermediate space.

That was the intermediate space; it came into being as *īkṣam*—for before that, this [space] had become visible (*īkṣam*) between [heaven and earth], and therefore it is called the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*). Now, when one has piled the Gārhapatya fire-altar and then piles the Āhavanīya, these two worlds were indeed first created; then, having returned, he pours out the Dhiṣṇya hearths for the sake of the continuity of the ritual action. Furthermore...
"When the two ends are indeed consecrated, the middle is consecrated.
7.2.1. [1] Now, therefore, they carry away the Nairṛta bricks. For the gods, having built the Gārhapatya altar, ascended it; this world, indeed, is the Gārhapatya.

Having consecrated this very world as the *gārhapatya* fire, they ascended it; they saw only that darkness, which was beyond the range of vision. They said, "Find a way so that we may drive away this darkness, this evil.
They said, "Meditate!"—by which they meant, "Seek a layer of construction"; "Construct it so that we may [dispel] this darkness. 7.2.1. [2]
"Let us drive away evil," they said. (7.2.1.3) Being thus conscious, they saw these bricks belonging to Nirṛti; they laid them down, and by means of them, they [dispelled] that darkness.
They struck away evil; for Nirṛti is indeed evil. Because they struck away evil, that is, Nirṛti, with these [verses], therefore these [verses] are addressed to Nirṛti.
Now, this very thing is performed.
What the gods did—this is indeed that darkness; that evil was driven away by the gods themselves.
When he now performs this, thinking, "I shall do what the gods did," he thereby drives away whatever evil and whatever destruction (nirṛti) there may be by means of these [verses]. That which...
By these [verses], he drives away evil and destruction; therefore, these are dedicated to Nirṛti. Furthermore, as to why they carry these [offerings] dedicated to Nirṛti.

When the gods restored Prajāpati after he had fallen apart, they poured him, who had become seed, into the fire-pan as a womb—for the fire-pan is indeed a womb. For him, they prepared this foundation in a year; this very world is that foundation. This world, indeed, is [the fire-pan].
He generated him in that Gārhapatya fire; whatever evil, whatever phlegm, whatever membrane, and whatever afterbirth there was of his, they drove it away from him by means of these [verses].
Because they drove away (apāghnan) his evil and destruction (nirṛti) by means of these, therefore these [verses] are addressed to Nirṛti. 7.2.1. [6]

In the same way, the sacrificer pours himself as seed into the fire-pan (ukhā) as a womb; for the fire-pan is indeed a womb. For him, she prepares this foundation after a year—this very world, for this world is indeed [the foundation].
The Gārhapatya fire begets him therein; whatever evil, whatever phlegm, whatever membrane, and whatever afterbirth there is of his, that it drives away from him by means of these [verses].
Because it thus drives away his evil and destruction (nirṛti) by means of these, therefore they are called *nairṛtya*. 7.2.1. [7]
They are a foot in measure; he thus places evil and destruction beneath his feet. They are without characteristic marks;
for that which does not exist is without characteristic marks—he thus makes that non-existent evil into destruction. They are baked with husks.
The *tuṣas* (husks) indeed belong to Nirṛti; thus, by means of those belonging to Nirṛti, he performs this rite belonging to Nirṛti. They are black, for that darkness was black;
moreover, Nirṛti is indeed black.
With them, they go toward this quarter.
This is indeed the direction of Nirṛti; thus he places Nirṛti in that very direction, the quarter of Nirṛti.

Where there is a self-made pit or a fissure in the ground, there he should place these bricks; or where the earth of this [ground] is split open, or where plants do not grow—there he seizes the misfortunes (nirṛti) of this [place], for it belongs to Nirṛti.
He places Nirṛti upon that ground; having made those [bricks] facing away, he lays them down as partakers of the world.
"The one who does not press [Soma], the one who does not sacrifice"—Nirṛti indeed attacks him who neither presses nor sacrifices.
"Follow the track of the thief," that is, "follow the track of the robber and follow the track of the thief.

And furthermore, "as a thief or a robber goes into hiding, so go into hiding for us"—that is, "go away from one who does not know this. "Homage be to thee, O goddess Nirṛti!"—that is, "homage be to you, O divine Destruction."
By means of the salutation (*namaskāra*), he indeed drives her away. 7.2.1.[10] "Homage to thee, O Nirṛti, of sharp splendor! For Nirṛti is indeed of sharp splendor; of her—
He pays homage to this with the words, "This iron bond, loosen it.

For indeed, Nirṛti binds him whom she binds with an iron bond. With the words, "In agreement with Yama and Yamī," Agni is indeed Yama and this earth is Yamī; for by these two everything here is held in check. "In agreement with these two"—this refers to [the bond] upon the highest firmament.
"Make him ascend"—the world of heaven is indeed the *nāka*; thus he means, "Make the sacrificer ascend to the world of heaven.
(7.2.1.11) "Into whose terrible mouth I offer thee"—Nirṛti is indeed terrible; he offers this into her mouth, that which belongs to her deity.

"He performs action for the relinquishing of these bonds"—by which bonds one becomes bound. "Thee whom people rejoice in as 'the Earth'"—this is indeed the Earth; he who exists, exists upon her. "I know thee thoroughly as Nirṛti"—that is to say, "I know thee completely as Destruction. This [Earth] indeed...
This indeed is Nirṛti; she fastens upon him who digs. Just as one would say, "You are so-and-so, the son of such-and-such; I know you;
do not harm me," even so does he say this. For one who is known and addressed does not cause harm.
He does not touch [the water].

Nirṛti is indeed evil; thinking, "Lest I be touched by evil," he does not set it down. Setting down is a firm foundation; thinking, "Lest I establish evil as a foundation," he does not recite the *sūdadohas* verse over it. The *sūdadohas* is indeed the vital breath (*prāṇa*);
thinking, "Lest I connect or join evil with the vital breath," [he does not recite it]. 7.2.1. [13]

Some place them facing downward on the far side, thinking, "Nirṛti is indeed evil; let us not follow after evil Nirṛti. One should not do so; one should place them facing away [from oneself], for thus one drives away that evil.
He drives away destruction (nirṛti).
7.2.1.[14] He lays down three bricks.
Agni is threefold; as great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, by that much alone [he does so].

He thereby drives away that evil, destruction. 7.2.1.[15] Then he places the stool, the sling, the cord for the gold plate, and the two *iṇḍva*-dice on the further side; for the noose belongs to Nirṛti.

It is from the noose of Nirṛti that one is released; for it is said, "The noose which the goddess Nirṛti bound upon your necks, which could not be untied"—by one who does not know thus, it indeed cannot be untied. "That noose of yours I loosen from the midst of life.
Agni, indeed, is life, and the middle of this is that which has been built as the Gārhapatya fire-altar, while that which has not yet been built is the end.

The Āhavanīya fire is therefore [the source]. Whether he who piles the fire-altar is young or old, [the text] says: "Not from the middle of life. Then [he says]: "Eat this food, being impelled. Food indeed is *pitu*; thus, "eat this food, being impelled" is what is meant.
With *triṣṭubh* verses [he does this]; the *triṣṭubh* is indeed a thunderbolt; by the thunderbolt he thus repels evil and destruction. 7.2.1. [16]

There are three bricks: the throne, the sling, and the loop for the gold plate; and two *iṇḍva* stones—thus there are eight. The Gāyatrī consists of eight syllables, and Agni is of Gāyatra nature. As great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, by that much he repels evil and destruction. 7.2.1 [17]
Then, in the middle, he pours out water from the *udacamasam* vessel.

Water is indeed a thunderbolt; by means of the thunderbolt, he thus interposes an obstacle against evil and misfortune (*nirṛti*). "Homage to prosperity, which has done this here"—with these words they rise up; for this [act] is first performed for the sake of prosperity.

The gods performed this rite; they offered this salutation to her (Bhūti). Indeed, he performs this rite for the sake of prosperity, and he offers this salutation to her. They return without looking back; thus, they cast off evil and misfortune without looking back. Having returned, he stands worshipping the fire.
Indeed, he does what is improper when he goes in this direction while the fire-altar is only half-built; he makes amends to that very fire for the sake of non-injury.
Furthermore, as to why he stands in adoration (upasthāna).
This world is indeed the Gārhapatya fire; the Gārhapatya is a firm foundation, for this earth is the firm foundation.
Now, when he goes toward that direction, it is as if he goes upon a pathless way. Therefore, when he worships [the fires], he returns toward this very foundation;
he thus establishes himself firmly upon this foundation. 7.2.1 [20]
"He is the dwelling-place, the gatherer of riches"—for this world is indeed a dwelling-place and a gatherer of riches.
"He beholds all forms with his powers"—that is to say, he beholds all forms with his powers. He is like the divine Savitṛ.
"Satyadharma Indra did not stand in the battle of the paths"—as the *yajus* formula is, so is its explanation (*bandhu*).
7.2.2.[1] Then he offers the *prāyaṇīya*. At the call for the preparer of the oblation (*haviṣkṛt*), he releases his speech; having released his speech—

He carries away the *stambayajus*; having carried away the *stambayajus*, and having enclosed [the altar] with the eastern enclosure and having drawn lines, he says, "Carry it away—three times," and the Āgnīdhra carries it away three times.
Having returned, he proceeds with the *prāyaṇīya* offering.
Having performed the Prāyaṇīya offering, he yokes the plough.
For when the gods were about to prepare him (Agni), they first gratified him with food;
in the same way, this sacrificer, being about to prepare him, first gratifies him with food by means of the plough.
This furrow is indeed *sera*; he thereby bestows *irā* (nourishment) upon him. It is made of *udumbara* wood;
the *udumbara* is indeed strength and sap; he thus endows him with strength and sap.
Having split the girdle made of muñja grass, which is threefold— the significance of which has been stated—
he stands behind the southern hip of the fire-altar,
facing the northern shoulder.
He consecrates the plough being yoked with the verse: "The sages yoke the ploughs; they stretch out the yokes separately.
Those who possess knowledge are the sages; they indeed yoke the plough and stretch out the yokes separately.
"The wise among the gods for the sake of bliss"—bliss is indeed the sacrifice; thus, "the wise among the gods stretching out the sacrifice. 7.2.2. [5]
"Yoke the ploughs, stretch out the yokes"—for they indeed yoke the ploughs and stretch out the yokes.
"Sow the seed here in the prepared womb"—for that which is the furrow is made into a womb for the seed; just as seed [would be lost] in what is not a womb...
"He shall surely pour down that which he sows in unploughed ground, and let there be abundance through our song"—for "song" (*gīr*) is indeed speech, and "abundance" (*śruṣṭi*) is food.
"May the sickle come nearer to the ripened grain"—for when food is ripe, then they handle it with the sickle.
With two verses he yokes [the plow]: with a *gāyatrī* and a *triṣṭubh*; the significance of this has been explained. 7.2.2. [6]

He yokes the right ox first, then the left; thus it is among the gods, otherwise among men. It consists of six oxen, or twelve oxen, or twenty-four oxen, according to the correspondence with the year. 7.2.2. [7]

Then he ploughs it. Ploughing is indeed food; for the gods, intending to prepare him [the altar], first placed food within him. In the same way, this [officiant], intending to prepare him, first places food within him. 7.2.2. [8]
He indeed draws out only the body;
he does not place that food into the wings and tail, but rather into the body.
For whatever food is placed into the body protects the body, and thereby the wings and tail; whereas that which is in the wings and tail does not [protect them].

Then he protects himself, but not the wings and tail. He ploughs the first furrow toward the east between the enclosing stones on the southern half of the fire-altar with the mantra: "For prosperity... (Śunaṃ su...).
"May the ploughshares furrow the earth; may the plowmen go forth happily with their oxen"—by saying "happily, happily," he indeed makes her prosper, for that which is prosperous is "happily.
Then [he sows] toward the north along the rear half.
"Let Sītā be anointed with ghee and honey"—as the *yajus* is, so is its significance. "Approved by all the gods and the Maruts"—for both the All-gods and the Maruts have power over the rain.
"Rich in vigor, swelling with milk"—milk is indeed sap; thus she is rich in vigor through sap, that is, through food.
"Swelling," that is to say, "O Sītā, turn toward us with milk"; "O Sītā, turn toward us with sap"—this is what it means.
7.2.2.[11] Then, with the second half-verse:
"The plough, sharp-edged," that is to say, "the plough, rich in wealth"; "well-favored."
"O you who are rich in Soma!"—Soma is indeed food; thus he scatters it. "A cow, a fat ewe, and a chariot with a seat"—for all this he scatters while moist.
Then, with the front half [of the formula], he scatters toward the south.

"Milk out desire, O yielder of desires, for Mitra and Varuṇa, for Indra and the two Aśvins, for Pūṣan, for progeny, and for the plants"—for agriculture indeed belongs to all the gods; "milk out all desires for these deities," he thereby says. Thus he plows first with "iti," then with "atha," then with "atha," then with "atha."
"He turns to the right, for that is the way among the gods. He ploughs four furrows with a sacrificial formula.
Thus, whatever food exists in the four quarters, he places that within him.
That indeed is truly by means of the *yajus*; for that which is the *yajus* is truly real, and these quarters are truly real. 7.2.2. [14] Then he draws out the self;
thereby he places in him whatever food there is in the year.
That which is silent is indeed unexpressed; and that which is silent is everything, for everything is unexpressed. Thus, he places this food in him by means of everything.
First he ploughs with "Thus," then with "Thus," then with "Thus," then with "Thus"—this is a turning to the right, for that is the way among the gods.
He ploughs three furrows each time.
Agni is threefold; as great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, with just that much he places this food in him.
He plows twelve furrows silently.
Twelve months make a year; the year is Agni. As great as Agni is, as great as is his measure, with just so much he places this food in him. These two groups together amount to sixteen.
Prajāpati consists of sixteen parts;
Prajāpati is Agni. Thus, he places in him food that is commensurate with his own self.
For that food which is commensurate with one's self protects it and does not harm it; that which is more harms it, and that which is less does not [suffice].
He protects it. Furthermore, when he draws it out, it is because the gods, while about to consecrate him, [did so].
In the beginning, they placed the vital breaths (prāṇas) in front; likewise, he, intending to consecrate this [earth], places the vital breaths in front.
There are furrows; for these vital breaths are indeed located in the furrows.
He plows four furrows with a sacrificial formula (yajus).

Now, those four vital breaths (prāṇas) which are defined as being in the head—this he places in him by means of the Yajus formula. For that which is the Yajus is indeed truth (addhā), and these vital breaths in the head are indeed truth. 7.2.2 [20]

Furthermore, as for why he draws out himself: he thereby places those very vital breaths (*prāṇa*) which are within the self into this [body]. He does so silently; for who knows how many these vital breaths within the self actually are? 7.2.2. [21]
Then he unyokes them:

"Having attained that desire for which you were yoked, be unyoked, O inviolable ones! For these are indeed inviolable among the gods; "O paths leading to the gods," for by means of these the divine rite is performed.
"He performs [the rite] with the words, 'We have gone to the further shore of this darkness. Darkness, indeed, is hunger; thus he says, 'We have gone to the further shore of this hunger.

'May we attain the light,' he says, for he who attains the gods and the sacrifice attains the light. Then he releases them toward the north-east; the significance of that has been explained. He gives them to the Adhvaryu, for it is he who performs them; but they belong to the sacrificial fees."
At the proper time, he should assign [the portions].
Then he places a bunch of *darbha* grass.
For it was this very thing that the gods placed down as the plants.
In the same way, the sacrificer places these plants;
and furthermore, as for why he places a bunch of *darbha* grass:
when this [Agni] is piled, he is being born, and he is born from everything.
It is born from food; both of these are indeed food: the *darbha* grasses and the waters, for these are both plants and waters.
Those waters which, loathing Vṛtra, welled up on the desert and became *darbha* grasses—because they welled up (*udāyan*) while scattering (*dṛbhanta*), therefore they are called *darbha*.
These *darbha* grasses are indeed pure and fit for sacrifice, being waters that have flowed forth from Vṛtra. Because they are *darbha*...
That there are *darbha* grasses: the plants are both [the giver and the receiver]; thus he gratifies me with this food from both sides.
At the "meeting of the furrows" (*sītāsamara*):
the meeting of the furrows is indeed speech; the furrows are the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), and this [meeting] is their union; for speech is indeed [superior] to the vital breaths.
Food is placed in the middle; verily, he thus places food in the very middle of him. He does so silently;
for that which is silent is undefined, and the undefined is everything; verily, by means of everything he thus bestows this food upon him.
Then he makes an offering over it.

This one is born when he is piled up; he is born for the sake of all food. This ghee is the essence of all this, for it is the essence of both the waters and the plants. He thus gratifies him with the essence of all this. As great as the essence is, so great is the self; he thus gratifies him with the essence of all this by means of his own self.

As great as essence is, so great is the self; by means of this entire [essence], he thus gratifies him. With [ghee] taken five times, for the fire-altar has five layers, the year has five seasons, and the year is Agni. As great as Agni is, as great as is his measure, with just so much food does he thus gratify him. 7.2.3. [5]
And as to why he offers over it:
when the Rishis, the vital breaths, first prepared this Agni,
they made him this share beforehand.

Therefore, there are portions for those in front; thus, when he makes offerings over it, he gratifies those very *ṛṣis* who were the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) and who made their portion in front. He does so with ghee taken five times; the significance of that has already been explained. Furthermore, as to why he makes offerings over it:
Indeed, whatever forms he is about to place upon this fire-altar—whatever *stomas*, whatever *pṛṣṭhas*, and whatever *chandas*—for these he makes this portion beforehand;
it is these very things that he gratifies with the fivefold-drawn clarified butter. The significance of this has already been explained. 7.2.3. [7]
And as to why he offers over it:
the gods were indeed afraid, thinking, "This ritual is long; surely the Rakṣases and the destroyers might strike down this [victim] here. They [performed] this [offering] for that ritual.
Not seeing its completion beforehand, they established it all right here and built it up right here;
in the same way, he now establishes it all right here and builds it up right here. 7.2.3. [8]
"United with the year" is the layer (*citi*);
"with the days" is the filling soil (*purīṣa*). "United with the Dawn" is the layer; "with the ruddy ones" is the filling soil.
"The two Aśvins, united" is the layer; "with their wondrous deeds" is the filling soil. "United with the Sun" is the layer; "with Etaśa" is the filling soil.
"United with Vaiśvānara" is the layer; "with Iḍā" is the filling; "with ghee" is the layer; "Sva" is the filling; "Ha" is the layer. These are thirteen utterances (*vyāhṛti*);
there are thirteen months.

The year consists of thirteen months; there are thirteen layers of earth (purīṣa) for the fire-altar. As great as Agni is, as great as his measure is—just so much does he thus build up. He offers with clarified butter; for this clarified butter is Agni: it is Agni whom he thus builds up.
With fivefold-drawn butter he offers, for the fire-altar has five layers, the year has five seasons, and the year is Agni.

"As great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, so much of him he thus piles up. Holding it upwards, he offers; for upwards indeed he piles Agni by means of the layers (citīḥ). 7.2.4 [1] Then he pours out the water-vessels.

The gods indeed said, "Reflect ye!"—by which they meant, "Seek a layer (citi). While reflecting, they perceived rain as the layer; they placed that into this [fire-altar], and in the same way, this [sacrificer] now places it into this [altar]. 7.2.4. [2]
There are water-cups.

Water is indeed rain; thus he bestows rain upon this [sacrificer]. With a cup made of Udumbara wood—its significance has already been explained—he uses one with four corners, for there are four quarters; [he does so] from all [the quarters].
Thus he bestows this rain upon it from all directions. He pours out three cups of water each time;
Agni is threefold—so great as Agni is, so great is his measure.
By that much alone he bestows this rain upon it. He pours out twelve water-cups on the ploughed ground;
twelve months are a year, and the year is [the sacrifice].
As great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, with just that much he bestows rain upon this [earth].
He pours it out on ploughed ground;
therefore it rains for the ploughed land. If he were to pour it out only on what is ploughed and not on what is unploughed...

He would rain only on what is ploughed, not on what is unploughed; and if he were to pour out [the water] only on unploughed ground and not on the ploughed, it would rain only on the ploughed, not on the unploughed.
But since he pours it out both on the ploughed and the unploughed, therefore it rains both on the ploughed and the unploughed.
He pours it out three times on both the ploughed and the unploughed.
Agni is threefold; as great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, with just that much he bestows rain upon him.
Furthermore, as to why he pours out the water-cups: it is for the sake of providing moisture.

The gods, when they were about to consecrate him, placed water in front of him; in the same way, this one, when he is about to consecrate him, places water in front of him. He pours out three by three handfuls of water.
Agni is threefold; as great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, with just that much he thus bestows water upon him.
He pours down twelve water-vessels on the ploughed ground.
Twelve months make a year; the year is Agni. As great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, with just so much does he thus bestow water upon him.
He pours it out on ploughed ground.

He places those waters in the vital breaths (*prāṇa*). If he were to pour them only on what is ploughed and not on what is unploughed, the waters would be in the vital breaths alone and not in the other part of the self. And if he were to pour them only on what is unploughed and not on what is ploughed, the waters would be in the self alone and not in the vital breaths. He pours them both on what is ploughed and on what is unploughed; therefore, these waters exist in both places.
And [he pours it] over the vital breaths and the self.
He pours it out three times on both the ploughed and the unploughed ground;
for Agni is threefold—so great is Agni, such is his measure.
By that much alone he places these waters in it.
He pours out fifteen water-cups;
for the thunderbolt is fifteenfold; by this very fifteenfold [thunderbolt] he [strikes] him.
With the *vajra*, he strikes away all evil. 7.2.4.[13] Then he sows all kinds of herbs.
Regarding this, the gods said, "Reflect!"—that is to say, "Seek a layer (*citi*)."
Being conscious of this, they saw food itself as the layer (citi); they placed it in him, and in the same way, this [priest] now places it in him.
It consists of all kinds of herbs.

All that food which consists of all herbs, he thereby places as food within this [person]. He should set aside one kind of that food and not eat it for as long as he lives. With a cup made of udumbara wood—its significance has already been explained—he [should drink]; it should have four corners, for there are four...

Verily, from all the quarters he thus bestows food upon him; he sows with *anuṣṭubh* verses, for the *anuṣṭubh* is speech, and it is by means of speech that food is eaten. He sows with three verses at a time.
Agni is threefold; as great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, with just that much he places this food in him.
With twelve verses he sows in the ploughed field.
Twelve months make a year; the year is Agni. As great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, with just that much he places this food in him.
He sows on ploughed ground.

Therefore, food ripens on ploughed ground; for if one were to sow only on ploughed ground and not on unploughed, food would ripen only on ploughed ground and not on unploughed. And if one were to sow only on unploughed ground and not on ploughed, food would ripen only on unploughed ground and not on ploughed. But since he sows both on ploughed and on unploughed ground, therefore food ripens both on ploughed and on unploughed ground. 7.2.4 [18]
With three [verses] he sows on both the ploughed and the unploughed ground.
Agni is threefold; as great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, with just that much he places this food in him. 7.2.4. [19]
And as to why he sows all kinds of herbs: when the gods were about to prepare him, they first healed him with every medicine;
in the same way, this sacrificer, being about to prepare him, first heals him with every medicine.
"He heals" (bhiṣajyati) [7.2.4.20]:
it becomes a medicine for all;
all this is a remedy, namely that which is a medicine for all.
He heals him with this entire medicine.
He sows with three verses each;
Agni is threefold—whatever is the extent of Agni, whatever is his measure.
By that much he heals him.
With twelve verses he sows on the ploughed ground; twelve months are a year, and the year is the whole.
"As great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, with just that much he heals him.
He sows on ploughed ground; thereby he heals the vital breaths. If he were to sow only on ploughed ground and not on unploughed, he would heal only the vital breaths."
If he were to sow only on unplowed ground and not on plowed ground, he would heal only himself and not the vital breaths;
but since he sows both on plowed and unplowed ground, he heals both the vital breaths and himself.
He sows on both the plowed and the unplowed with three [verses].
Agni is threefold; as great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, by that much he heals him.
He pours out fifteen water-jars and sows with fifteen verses; that makes thirty, for the *triṣṭubh* consists of thirty syllables.
The Virāj is the Virāj; it is food in its entirety. He thus places this entire food within him.
(7.2.4) "The plants that were born first, three ages before the gods"—the gods are indeed the seasons; he offers these [plants] to them three times.

Formerly they were born in spring, in the rainy season, and in autumn. "Of the brown ones, I am one," [he says]. Soma is indeed brown; plants belong to Soma, and man consists of plants. "A hundred abodes"—this refers to the fact that he has a hundred-year lifespan, a hundredfold value, and a hundredfold strength; these are his hundred abodes. "And seven"—these are the seven [vital breaths] which are here.
"The vital breaths are in the head; it is of these that he speaks when he says (VS 32.4):
'A hundred, O Mother, are your stations, and a thousand are your growths,' which refers to these [channels] that are a hundredfold and a thousandfold."
"O you of a hundred powers, having grown up, make this man of mine free from disease"—that is to say, "this one whom I am healing.
These [verses] have a single explanation;
they refer to this very [person], just as one would heal this one and bring him across; these are *anuṣṭubh* verses.
For speech is the anuṣṭubh, and speech is every remedy; thus, by means of every remedy, he heals him.
Now, therefore, regarding those [verses] that are both expressed and unexpressed.

With a *yajus* formula he yokes two oxen, and the others silently; with a *yajus* formula he plows four furrows, and the others silently; silently he places a bunch of *darbha* grass, and with a *yajus* formula he makes an offering over it; silently he pours out the water-jars, and with a *yajus* formula he sows the seed. 7.2.4. [30]
This Agni is Prajāpati;
for Prajāpati is both the defined and the undefined, the limited and the unlimited. Thus, when he performs with a Yajus formula, that which is his defined and limited form [is thereby established].
He completes this [sacrifice] for him by means of that; and what is done silently—that which is its unexpressed, unlimited form—he completes for him by means of that.

Indeed, he who, knowing this, performs it in this manner, completes this Prajāpati in his entirety. The external forms are expressed, while the internal ones are unexpressed; this [sacrifice] is a living creature (paśu).
Since it is Agni, therefore the external forms of the animal are expressed (nirukta), while the internal ones are unexpressed (anirukta). 7.3.1.
[1] The Gārhapatya fire-altar is built up, while the Āhavanīya is not built up; then he purchases the King (Soma). This world, indeed, is...
The Gārhapatya fire is the sky, and the Āhavanīya fire is the heaven; and that wind which blows here is this Soma.
He thus places him between these two worlds, and therefore this [wind] blows between these two worlds.
Furthermore, as for the fact that [the fire] is piled upon the Gārhapatya...

When the Āhavanīya fire has been piled, he then purchases the King (Soma). Agni is indeed the self and Soma is the vital breath; thus, he places that vital breath in the middle of the self. Therefore, this vital breath is in the middle of this self. Furthermore, when the Gārhapatya fire has been piled:
When the Āhavanīya fire has been piled, he then purchases the King (Soma). The fire is indeed the self and Soma is the essence;
thus he unites the self with its essence. Therefore, this very self is permeated through and through by its essence.
Having purchased the King and carried him around, [he proceeds].

Then he prepares for him the guest-offering (ātithya-havis). At the call to the preparer of the oblation (haviṣkṛt), he releases his speech; and thus he interlinks the ritual of the sacrifice (adhvara-karma) and the ritual of the fire-altar (agni-karma) for the sake of the uniformity of the rite, so that "this rite may be one and the same. 7.3.1. [5]

Moreover, as to why he interlinks [the verses]: the fire-altar is indeed the self, and the sacrifice is the vital breath; he thus places the vital breath in the middle of the self. Therefore, this vital breath is in the middle of the self. 7.3.1.6.
Moreover, as to why he interlinks [the two fires]:
the fire-altar is indeed the self and the sacrifice is the essence; he thus attaches the self to the essence.
Therefore, this very self is attached to its extremity by means of the essence. Then he goes halfway toward the Āhavanīya fire.
Now, some indeed sweep away with a *palāśa* branch on both occasions, saying, "On both occasions he piles [the fire]. One should not do so;
for by means of the *gārhapatya* one settles down, while by means of the *āhavanīya* one rises upward. Therefore, one should not do so.
Then, he pours out the soil for the *uṣas* on the *gārhapatya* itself.
He does not place it on the Āhavanīya; for the Gārhapatya is this world, and the saline soil (ūṣā) is cattle;
he thus places cattle in this world, and therefore these cattle are found in this world. 7.3.1.
[9] Then he places the lotus-leaf on the Āhavanīya itself.

Not on the Gārhapatya; for the lotus leaf is indeed the waters, and the Āhavanīya is the sky; he thus places the waters in the sky. On both occasions he scatters sand; for sand is seed, and it is on both occasions that [the embryo] is transformed. Thus, [he does this] so that there may be transformation from that seed. 7.3.1. [10]
He scatters them with two different formulas.

The Gārhapatya is indeed the world of men, and the Āhavanīya is the world of the gods; for these two are distinct—the divine and the human—and he scatters [the grains] over the Āhavanīya with a longer formula.
For the lifespan of the gods is longer and the lifespan of humans is shorter;
he pours sand into the *gārhapatya* fire before the enclosing stones (*pariśrit*), for sand is seed; [he does this] so that from this seed these various transformations may proceed.

Regarding this they say: "The enclosing-stones are the womb and the sand is the seed; now, since he first pours the sand on the Gārhapatya fire before the enclosing-stones, how is it that his seed becomes enclosed without being spilled?
The saline soil (ūṣa) is indeed the amnion; thus, when he first pours down the saline soil, by means of this amnion his seed becomes enclosed without being spilled.

When it has been prepared, he consecrates the enclosing stones; the significance of this has already been explained. Then he pours down sand; sand is indeed seed; thus his seed, poured into this womb, becomes enclosed. 7.3.1. [12] Then he touches the Āhavanīya fire with two verses containing the word *āpyāna*.
Not on the *gārhapatya* fire;

for the *gārhapatya* is this world, and the *āhavanīya* is the heavenly world. Now, the sacrificer has indeed been born in this world, and it is in the heavenly world that he is to be brought forth. Therefore, when he touches [the fire] with the two "swelling" verses, he does so only at the *āhavanīya*, not at the *gārhapatya*.
In the *gārhapatya* fire, he thereby causes him to be born in that world, the heavenly realm.
Then he lays down the *logeṣṭakā* bricks. These worlds indeed are this Agni; the quarters are the *logeṣṭakā* bricks; [he thus places him] in these worlds.
He establishes the quarters; therefore, these quarters exist within these worlds.
7.3.1.[14] He brings [the earth] from outside the fire-altar.
Those quarters which are within these worlds have indeed been obtained by him; now, those which are beyond these worlds—
He places those quarters in this [fire-altar]. 7.3.1.
[15] This [altar] is outside the sacrificial ground; for this altar is indeed this earth.
Those quarters of his which are within it have already been obtained by him; but those quarters which are beyond this earth—those he now obtains.
In this [brick], he places this.
7.3.1.[16] Furthermore, as to why he lays down the *logeṣṭakā* bricks:
when Prajāpati had become relaxed, his vital essence flowed out in all directions.
Where the gods prepared [the fire-altar], they placed that essence into it by means of these brick-enclosures; in the same way, this [sacrificer] now places it into this [altar].
He brings [the earth] from outside the fire.
Or rather, that essence of his which is in these worlds—that essence which has flowed away beyond these worlds—he places it therein.
Outside the altar; for this altar is indeed this [earth]. 7.3.1. [18]
That essence of his which was in this [earth] is indeed obtained by him; and that essence which flowed away from her, he now places back into it.
He takes it up with the wooden sword (sphya).
The wooden sword (sphya) is indeed a thunderbolt (vajra), and the thunderbolt is strength; this earth is what is acquired through strength, for by means of strength one finds what is to be acquired.
7.3.1.[20] He brings it from the east, saying:
"May he who is the progenitor of the earth not harm me. Prajāpati, indeed, is the progenitor of the earth.

"May Prajāpati not harm us"—this means [the same]. "He who, possessing the law of truth, pervaded the sky"—this means "he who created the sky possessing the law of truth. "And he who first generated the shining waters"—the shining waters are indeed human beings; thus, it means "he who first created human beings. "To which god shall we offer worship with oblation?"—Prajāpati, indeed, is that god.
"How shall we worship him with an oblation?"—having brought that [brick], he places it within the enclosing stones upon his own body;
he thereby bestows in this [altar] whatever essence had flowed away in the eastern direction, and thus he bestows the eastern direction itself in this [altar]. 7.3.1. [21]
Then on the south side:
"Turn toward us, O Earth, with sacrifice and with milk"—as the sacrificial formula is, so is its significance.
"May Agni, impelled, ascend thy omentum"—whatever indeed is upon her, that is her omentum; that Agni, being impelled, [ascends].

It grows while burning; having taken that [earth], he places it within himself between the two joints of the wings. Whatever essence flowed away in the southern direction, that he now places in this [altar]; moreover, he thereby bestows the southern quarter upon it. 7.3.1. [22] Then towards the west.

"O Agni, that which is thy bright, that which is thy radiant, that which is thy pure, and that which is thy worthy of sacrifice"—this earth, indeed, is Agni; he thus speaks of her. "We bring that for the gods"—that is to say, "we bring that for this divine work.
Having brought it, he places it within the junction of the tail upon the body. That essence which was in the western quarter—
He places this [earth] in it; thus he bestows upon it this very western quarter.
He should not bring it from directly behind, lest he should bring the essence away from the path of the sacrifice; rather, he brings it as if from a distance.
Then, from the north.
"I have taken nourishment and strength from here"—this means "I have taken nourishment and strength from here.

"The womb of *ṛta*": *ṛta* is indeed truth; thus, "the womb of truth. "The stream of the buffalo": the buffalo is indeed Agni, for once born, he pervaded all this greatness. "May it enter me in my cattle and in my bodies"—"body" (*tanū*) is indeed the self (*ātman*); thus, "may it enter me."
"May it enter into the cows and into myself"—saying this, he pours it out; "I abandon exhaustion, want, and disease"—saying this, he scatters the sand.
Thus, whatever exhaustion, want, and disease there was, he places that in this direction; therefore, in this direction creatures are hungry.
Having brought that [sand] back, he lays it down upon himself between the two joints of the wings. That which is the essence in the northern direction—
He places this [brick] in this [corner]; thus he bestows the northern quarter upon it.
These are the quarters;
he lays them down on all sides; thus he bestows the quarters on every side. Therefore, the quarters are on every side.

He places them facing toward all directions; therefore the quarters face toward all [points]. He lays them down separately, settles them separately, and pronounces the *sūdadohas* verse over them separately, for the quarters are separate. Standing, he lays them down, for the quarters are, as it were, standing; moreover, one who stands is indeed more vigorous. 7.3.1. [25]

These are the bricks possessed of sacrificial formulas (yajuṣmatya iṣṭakāḥ). He places them only in the body (ātman), not in the wings or the tail; for it is in the body that the bricks possessed of sacrificial formulas are placed, and not in the wings or the tail. 7.3.1 [26]

Regarding this they say: "How do these [oblations] become cooked, prepared, and offered? Indeed, these are the essence, for the essence is self-cooked; moreover, whatever comes into contact with this Agni Vaiśvānara, that very thing becomes cooked, prepared, and offered. 7.3.1. [27]
Then he pours out the Uttaravedi.
This Vedi is indeed this earth, and the Uttaravedi is the sky; the *logeṣṭakās* are the quarters.
Thus, when he places the *logeṣṭakās* between the Vedi and the Uttaravedi, he places the quarters between these two worlds.

Therefore, he makes these two worlds separated by the quarters, either a distance of a *yuga* on all sides or forty paces, whichever he may desire; then he scatters sand, the significance of which has been explained.
He scatters it upon the high altar (*uttaravedi*).

The high altar (uttaravedi) is indeed the womb; he pours that seed into the womb. For whatever seed is poured into the womb becomes capable of procreation. With those [bricks], he covers his entire self;
he places that seed in his entire self. Therefore, seed arises from every part of the self. 7.3.1 [29]

"O Agni, yours is glory and vigor"— for smoke is indeed his glory and vigor, since it makes him heard in yonder world. "Greatly shine forth your rays, O radiant one"— for great indeed are his shining rays.

"O most excellent Savitṛ, O you of great luster, with power bestow food worthy of praise"—power indeed is strength; "with strength, O you of great luster, bestow food worthy of praise"—this is what it means. "To the donor, O wise one"—the donor is indeed the sacrificer; "to the sacrificer, O wise one, you bestow"—this is what it means. 7.3.1 [30]

"Possessing purifying luster, possessing bright luster"—for he indeed possesses purifying luster and bright luster; "with undiminished luster you rise up with your light"—that is, "you shine forth with your light with undiminished luster"; "moving between the two mothers, the son, you wait upon them"—the son [is Agni].
"Truly, moving between the two mothers, he protects them; you fill both worlds. These two are indeed heaven and earth, the *rodasī*;
he fills both of them—yonder one with smoke and this one with rain.
"O Son of Strength, O Jātavedas, with excellent praises..."
"O Son of Strength, Jātavedas, with fair praises"—this means "rejoice with our insights.

"'Be well-disposed through our insights'—this means 'shine forth, being well-disposed through our insights. "'In thee they have placed abundant nourishments, O thou of many forms'—this means 'in thee they have placed nourishments of many aspects. "'Of wondrous aid, born of the lovely one'—the significance of this is exactly as the sacrificial formula [yajus] itself. 7.3.1. [32]

"O Agni, ruling over [the world], spread yourself out with living beings"—living beings, indeed, are human beings; thus, "O shining Agni, spread yourself out with humans. "To us, immortal wealth"—to us, riches.

"Bearing this immortal form, you shine forth"—for he indeed shines forth with this visible form. "You fulfill the winning power"—that is to say, you fulfill the eternal power. "The wise ordainer of the sacrifice. 7.3.1 [33] "The wise ordainer of the sacrifice."

"Adhvara" is indeed the sacrifice; "the ordainer of the sacrifice, the wise one"—this refers to him. "Dwelling in great wealth"—this means dwelling in great prosperity. "The gift of lovely fortune, the great nourishment"—this refers to the gift of lovely fortune.

"Great food"—this means "you bestow winning wealth"; "winning wealth"—this means "you bestow eternal wealth. "The upholder of *ṛta*"—this means "the upholder of truth. "The mighty one"—Agni indeed is the mighty one. "Visible to all"—[this is said of him].
"For he is visible to all; men have placed Agni in front for the sake of bliss"—bliss, indeed, is the sacrifice; thus they place him in front for the sake of the sacrifice.

"Thee, the far-hearing and most extensive, the divine one, with our song, O men, in age after age"—that is to say, "thee, the far-hearing and most extensive, the god, we men invoke with our song. 7.3.1 [35]
This very Agni Vaiśvānara is indeed this [altar].
These sand grains are scattered for the sake of commencing; by means of this six-verse hymn, he pours Agni Vaiśvānara himself, as seed, into him. There are six seasons in the year.

The year is Vaiśvānara. Regarding this they say: "Since sand is called *sikatā*, what is the form of their seed (*retas*)? One should reply: "White," for seed is white; and also "speckled," for seed is, as it were, speckled.
Regarding this they say: "When he scatters dry sand over moist seed, how do these [sand grains] become moist, taking on the form of seed?
The meters (*candāṃsi*) are indeed sap; and sap is moist. Thus, when he scatters them with the meters, in this way they become moist for him, taking on the form of seed. 7.3.1. [38]
Regarding this they say: "How are these [sand grains] of his placed by means of day and night? Day and night are indeed two: the bright and the dark;
the two sands are the white and the black. Thus, indeed, are these [grains] of his placed by means of day and night.

Regarding this they say: "How is it that these [sand-grains] of his are laid down in correspondence with the days and nights, neither deficient nor excessive? The days and nights are indeed infinite, and the sand-grains are infinite; thus, in this way, these of his are laid down in correspondence with the days and nights, neither deficient nor excessive. Now, why is it called "the oceanic chant" (*samudriyaṃ canda*)? It is because it is infinite.

The ocean has endless sands; that is the *canda* metre belonging to the ocean. Regarding this, they ask: "How is it that these [sand-bricks] come to be laid down separately and diversely by means of the *yajus*-formulas? The *yajus* is indeed the mind (*manas*).
This very mind, as the *yajus*, pervades all the sands. Thus, indeed, these [bricks] of his come to be laid down separately and diversely.
They are established with *yajus*-verses (7.3.1).

Regarding this, they say: "How is it that these [bricks] of his are established with all the *chandas*? It is because when he scatters them with this six-verse hymn, as many syllables as there are in the seven *chandas*, so many are there in this [hymn].
Thus, indeed, these [bricks] of his come to be laid down with all the meters by means of the syllables of the six-verse hymn.
Furthermore, as to why he scatters sand:
this Agni is Prajāpati, and the Brahman is everything.

Prajāpati—this very thing is that which was lost from the Brahman, namely the sand; and that which was not lost is this Agni who is being built up. When he scatters the sand, he thereby restores to him that which was lost from the Brahman. He scatters them uncounted and unlimited; for who indeed knows that?
As long as that [sacrificial ground] of Brahmā was destroyed, he who, knowing this, scatters sand, indeed restores this entire Prajāpati in its completeness.
Regarding this they say: "What is the number of these sands, which are beyond counting? One should say, "Two," for there are two kinds of sand: the white and the black.
And one should say, "Twenty-seven hundred," for so many are the days and nights of the year;
and "Two hundred and fifty-two," for so many are the syllables of this six-verse hymn;
and "Twenty-five," for semen is twenty-fivefold.
These are the bricks possessed of sacrificial formulas (*yajurmatī*).
He places them only in the body, not in the wings or the tail;
for it is in the body that the bricks possessed of sacrificial formulas are placed, not in the wings or the tail. He does not settle them, lest he should [destroy] the seed and procreation.
"Let me establish them," [he says].
7.3.1.[45] Then he touches them with two verses containing the word "swelling" (*āpyāna*);
he thereby causes this very seed that has been poured out to swell.
Therefore, the semen, once cast into the womb, is nourished by means of the two verses addressed to Soma. Soma is indeed breath; he thus places breath into the semen.
Therefore, the semen, once cast, comes into being together with breath; for it would indeed putrefy if it were to come into being without breath.
This very *sūdadohas* verse here is breath; Soma is breath, and the *sūdadohas* is breath. 7.3.1 [46]
"Swell up;
let virility come to you from every side, O Soma"—virility is indeed seed; thus, "swell up;
let your seed come to you from all sides, O Soma. "Be present at the gathering of strength"—strength is indeed food; thus, "be present at the gathering of food."
"Come together"—this [is the meaning]. "Together let thy milks, and thy strengths come together"—milk is indeed sap, and strengths are food; thus, "let thy saps and foods come together.

"Together, O thou who overcomest the hostile with manly power"—this means "together let the seeds overcome evil. "Swelling for immortality, O Soma"—he thereby places immortality in procreation; therefore, procreation is immortal.

"Place the highest glories in heaven!"—the moon, indeed, is his highest glory in heaven, for it makes him famous in yonder world. He causes it to swell with two verses, a *gāyatrī* and a *triṣṭubh*; the significance of this has been explained. 7.3.1 [47]
Now, therefore, follows the attainment of perfection.
He lays down four earth-bricks; he scatters [the sand] with a six-verse hymn;
he causes it to swell with two verses. That makes twelve; twelve months are a year; the year is...
"As great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, so great does that become.
Having touched [the fire] with the two verses containing the word "swelling" (*āpyānavatī*), he returns and proceeds with the *ātithya* offering; having proceeded with the *ātithya* offering...

He proceeds with the Pravargya and Upasad rites; having performed the Pravargya and Upasad rites, they then settle this layer upon the hide. As for why it is on a hide: the hide is indeed form, for the attainment of forms. It is on the hairy side; hair is indeed form, for the attainment of forms. It is on a red hide; for on the red hide all forms are present, for the attainment of all forms.
The ox is Agni; [he uses] an ox for the attainment of the forms of Agni. It has its neck facing east, for that is the manner among the gods.
He spreads it in front of the Gārhapatya fire, within the altar, with the hair upwards and the neck facing east; he thereby prepares this layer.
Then they settle it together and sprinkle it. As to why he sprinkles it: he thereby makes it pure and fit for sacrifice;

he does so with clarified butter (*ājya*), for that is pure and fit for sacrifice. Moreover, it is to prevent [the sacrificer] from ascending again, for no other oblation whatsoever is ever sprinkled with clarified butter. He does so silently; for that which is silent is undefined, and the undefined is indeed everything.

By this undefined [formula], he makes all of it pure and fit for sacrifice; furthermore, it is to prevent re-ascension, for they do not sprinkle any other sacrificial substance silently. Moreover, as to why he sprinkles: it is because of the breaths. For the breaths are undefined, since they are not defined by name. He thus places the breaths into himself. Therefore, one should breathe in and out through both nostrils. This is why he sprinkles. Furthermore, as to why he sprinkles: it is for the sake of consecration (*dīkṣā*). For the breaths are consecrated; he thus bestows the consecration upon himself. Therefore, one should breathe in and out through both nostrils. This is why he sprinkles. Furthermore, as to why he sprinkles: it is for the sake of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). For the breaths are the sacrificial fee; he thus bestows the sacrificial fee upon himself. Therefore, one should breathe in and out through both nostrils. This is why he sprinkles. Furthermore, as to why he sprinkles: it is for the sake of the sacrificial food (*havis*). For the breaths are the sacrificial food; he thus bestows the sacrificial food upon himself. Therefore, one should breathe in and out through both nostrils. This is why he sprinkles. Furthermore, as to why he sprinkles: it is for the sake of the world. For the breaths are the world; he thus wins the world for himself. Therefore, one should breathe in and out through both nostrils. This is why he sprinkles. Furthermore, as to why he sprinkles: it is for the sake of the gods. For the breaths are the gods; he thus wins the gods for himself. Therefore, one should breathe in and out through both nostrils. This is why he sprinkles. Furthermore, as to why he sprinkles: it is for the sake of the self. For the breaths are the self; he thus wins the self for himself. Therefore, one should breathe in and out through both nostrils. This is why he sprinkles. Furthermore, as to why he sprinkles: it is for the sake of offspring. For the breaths are offspring; he thus wins offspring for himself. Therefore, one should breathe in and out through both nostrils. This is why he sprinkles. Furthermore, as to why he sprinkles: it is for the sake of cattle. For the breaths are cattle; he thus wins cattle for himself. Therefore, one should breathe in and out through both nostrils. This is why he sprinkles. Furthermore, as to why he sprinkles: it is for the sake of the All. For the breaths are the All; he thus wins the All for himself. Therefore, one should breathe in and out through both nostrils. This is why he sprinkles. Furthermore, as to why he sprinkles: it is for the sake of immortality. For the breaths are immortality; he thus wins immortality for himself.
