Therefore, one should breathe in and out through both nostrils. This is why he sprinkles. Furthermore, as to why he sprinkles: it is for the sake of the sun. For the breaths are the sun; he thus wins the sun for himself. Therefore, one should breathe in and out through both nostrils. This is why he sprinkles. Furthermore, as to why he sprinkles: it is for the sake of the moon. For the breaths are the moon; he thus wins the moon for himself. Therefore, one should breathe in and out through both nostrils. This is why he sprinkles. Furthermore, as to why he sprinkles: it is for the sake of the stars. For the breaths are the stars; he thus wins the stars for himself. Therefore, one should breathe in and out through both nostrils. This is why he sprinkles. Furthermore, as to why he sprinkles: it is for the sake of the waters. For the breaths are the waters; he thus wins the waters for himself. Therefore, one should breathe in and out through both nostrils. This is why he sprinkles. Furthermore, as to why he sprinkles: it is for the sake of the plants. For the breaths are the plants; he thus wins the plants for himself. Therefore, one should breathe in and out through both nostrils. This is why he sprinkles. Furthermore, as to why he sprinkles: it is for the sake of the fire. For the breaths are the fire; he thus wins the fire for himself. Therefore, one should breathe in and out through both nostrils. This is why he sprinkles. Furthermore, as to why he sprinkles: it is for the sake of the wind. For the breaths are the wind; he thus wins the wind for himself. Therefore, one should breathe in and out through both nostrils. This is why he sprinkles. Furthermore, as to why he sprinkles: it is for the sake of the sky. For the breaths are the sky; he thus wins the sky for himself. Therefore, one should breathe in and out through both nostrils. This is why he sprinkles. Furthermore, as to why he sprinkles: it is for the sake of the earth. For the breaths are the earth; he thus wins the earth for himself. Therefore, one should breathe in and out through both nostrils. This is why he sprinkles. Furthermore, as to why he sprinkles: it is for the sake of the intermediate region. For the breaths are the intermediate region; he thus wins the intermediate region for himself. Therefore, one should breathe in and out through both nostrils. This is why he sprinkles. Furthermore, as to why he sprinkles: it is for the sake of the quarters. For the breaths are the quarters; he thus wins the quarters for himself. Therefore, one should breathe in and out through both nostrils. This is why he sprinkles. Furthermore, as to why he sprinkles: it is for the sake of the *ṛc*. For the breaths are the *ṛc*; he thus wins the *ṛc* for himself. Therefore, one should breathe in and out through both nostrils. This is why he sprinkles. Furthermore, as to why he sprinkles: it is for the sake of the *sāman*. For the breaths are the *sāman*; he thus wins the *sāman* for himself. Therefore, one should breathe in and out through both nostrils. This is why he sprinkles. Furthermore, as to why he sprinkles: it is for the sake of the *yajus*. For the breaths are the *yajus*; he thus wins the *yajus* for himself. Therefore, one should breathe in and out through both nostrils. This is why he sprinkles. Furthermore, as to why he sprinkles: it is for the sake of the *brahman*. For the breaths are the *brahman*; he thus wins the *brahman* for himself. Therefore, one should breathe in and out through both nostrils. This is why he sprinkles. Furthermore, as to why he sprinkles: it is for the sake of the *kṣatra*. For the breaths are the *kṣatra*; he thus wins the *kṣatra* for himself. Therefore, one should breathe in and out through both nostrils. This is why he sprinkles. Furthermore, as to why he sprinkles: it is for the sake of the *viś*. For the breaths are the *viś*; he thus wins the *viś* for himself. Therefore, one should breathe in and out through both nostrils. This is why he sprinkles. Furthermore, as to why he sprinkles: it is for the sake of the *satyam*. For the breaths are the *satyam*; he thus wins the *satyam* for himself. Therefore, one should breathe in and out through both nostrils. This is why he sprinkles. Furthermore, as to why he sprinkles: it is for the sake of the *ṛtam*. For the breaths are the *ṛtam*; he thus wins the *ṛtam* for himself. Therefore, one should breathe in and out through both nostrils. This is why he sprinkles. Furthermore, as to why he sprinkles: it is for the sake of the *bhūtam*. For the breaths are the *bhūtam*; he thus wins the *bhūtam* for himself. Therefore, one should breathe in and out through both nostrils. This is why he sprinkles. Furthermore, as to why he sprinkles: it is for the sake of the *bhaviṣyat*. For the breaths are the *bhaviṣyat*; he thus wins the *bhaviṣyat* for himself. Therefore, one should breathe in and out through both nostrils. This is why he sprinkles. Furthermore, as to why he sprinkles: it is for the sake of the past. For the breaths are the past; he thus wins the past for himself. Therefore, one should breathe in and out through both nostrils. This is why he sprinkles. Furthermore, as to why he sprinkles: it is for the sake of the future. For the breaths are the future; he thus wins the future for himself. Therefore, one should breathe in and out through both nostrils. This is why he sprinkles. Furthermore, as to why he sprinkles: it is for the sake of the present. For
This is indeed an oblation; he sprinkles it with this [ghee].

For that which is anointed and that which is sprinkled is acceptable and fit for sacrifice. It is with ghee, for they sprinkle the oblation with ghee. It is silently, for they sprinkle the oblation silently.
He does so with *darbha* grasses, for they are pure and fit for sacrifice; with the tips, for the tip belongs to the gods. 7.3.2. [4]

Regarding this they say: "Since he sprinkles only the first layer, how does this entire Agni become sprinkled? How is it led forward upon the skin? How is it led forward by the horse? In that he sprinkles the bricks of all the layers here, in this way indeed his entire Agni becomes sprinkled; in this way [it is] upon the skin.
Thus, being excellent, the excellent horse exerts itself toward this layer.
Then he says, "Recite for the fires as they are being cast forward.
For the gods, when about to go forth, [prepared] this...
As they were stretching out that sacrifice, the destructive *rakṣas* demons sought to strike them, thinking, "You shall not sacrifice; you shall not stretch out the sacrifice!

Having fashioned these fires as these bricks—thunderbolts with razor-sharp edges—they hurled them at them. With these they struck them down; having struck them down, they performed this sacrifice in a place free from danger and destruction. 7.3.2. [6]
This very thing is done now which the gods did then; indeed, those *rakṣas* were already struck down by the gods themselves.
But when he performs this [rite], it is with the thought, "I shall do what the gods did," and furthermore, [it is] against whatever *rakṣas* or whatever evil there may be from them.
Having made these fires and these bricks into thunderbolts with razor-sharp edges, he hurls them; with them he strews over those [obstacles].
Having strewn them, he extends this sacrifice in a place free from danger and free from destructive spirits.
As for the words "to the fires": it is because they are indeed fires.
For these layers are indeed many fires; and as for [the formula] "to those being hurled," he does indeed hurl them forth. Regarding this, some recite the following: 7.3.2.[8]
"The fires dwelling in the soil, in harmony with the downward-flowing streams"—this has the form of departure; he should not do it thus.

He should rather recite Gāyatrī verses addressed to Agni that contain [words of] desire: "May Vatsa direct his mind toward thee," "To thee, O best of Aṅgirases," and "Agni in his dear abodes. 7.3.2. [9]
He recites verses addressed to Agni, for the attainment of the forms of Agni; they are full of desire, for the attainment of desires; they are in the Gāyatrī metre, for Agni is of Gāyatrī nature;
as great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, by that much he pours him out as seed.
The Agni consists of three *trivṛt* [stomas]; as great as the Agni is, as great as his measure is, with just that much he pours him out as seed.
These amount to seven, together with the two [verses] recited three times; the Agni has seven layers, there are seven seasons in the year, and the year is the Agni.
As great as the Agni is, as great as his measure is, so great does that become. He recites them in a low voice (*upāṃśu*), for here it is seed.
In the sacrifice, the seed is indeed poured out in a whisper; following behind while reciting, he goes along protecting the sacrifice from behind by means of the meters.
Then they lead a white horse in front.

The gods were indeed afraid, thinking, "Lest the *rakṣases* and destroyers (*nāṣṭrās*) here slay us. They saw this thunderbolt—namely, yonder sun; for yonder sun is this horse. Having struck away the *rakṣases* and destroyers from the front with this thunderbolt, they [attained] safety in a place free from danger and destruction.

In the same way, the sacrificer, having struck away the *rakṣases* and the *nāṣṭrās* from the front with this thunderbolt, attains well-being in a state free from danger and destruction; they approach the fire, placing the layer of the tail on the south side and making the horse step upon it on the north side. 7.3.2. [11]
They lead him eastward from the northern shoulder of the fire-altar, between the enclosing stones;
thereby he drives away evil from the eastern quarter. They lead him southward; thereby he drives away evil from the southern quarter. They lead him...

He drives away evil from that [spot] toward the western direction; he drives away evil from that toward the northern direction. Having thus driven away the Rakṣases and the destroyers from all these directions, he then lets it go northward and eastward; the significance of this has already been explained. 7.3.2. [12]

As he goes toward the west, he causes the horse to smell this layer. For that horse is yonder sun, and all these creatures which are these bricks are these very creatures; thus, when he makes it smell, yonder sun thereby [smells] these creatures.

He smells it; therefore, he thinks, "I am indeed all this," by means of Prajāpati’s vital power. Now, as to why he makes him smell it while moving westward: for as he moves westward, he smells all these creatures. And furthermore, as to why he makes him smell it.
Yonder sun is this horse, and these worlds are these *svayamātṛṇṇā* bricks. When he makes [the horse] smell them, yonder sun thereby winds these worlds together upon a thread;
that which is the thread above is its significance. 7.3.2. [14]
Furthermore, as to why he causes him to smell [the oblation]:
Agni went up from the gods and entered the waters. Those gods said to Prajāpati, "Search for this one; he will manifest himself to you, his own father."
The horse, having become white, sought him out; he found him who had crept up from the waters onto a lotus leaf. He looked down at him, and it scorched him; therefore it scorched him.
Therefore the white horse has a face as if scorched, and its eyes are likely to be bad. For they [the other horses] were indeed intent on injuring or harming him.

He said, "I grant you a boon. He replied, "Whoever seeks you by means of this form shall indeed find you. Verily, whoever seeks him by means of this form finds him; having found him, he builds him up.
It should be white;
for that which shines yonder is indeed its form. If he cannot find a white one, it may even be non-white;
however, it should be a horse. If he cannot find a horse, it may even be an ox, or one belonging to Agni.
The ox is Agni, the remover of all evils. 7.3.2.
[17] Now, therefore, regarding the mounting itself:
some indeed mount it from the front facing backward, or from the back facing forward.

One should not do so; for this Agni is a beast. Indeed, he who mounts the beast from the front toward the back kills it with its two horns; but he who mounts it from behind toward the front mounts it with his own self by means of its feet. Verily, he who mounts a beast with his own self reaches the further shore, and he does not perish.

For whatever animal they mount from the north, he destroys it; therefore they mount it from the north itself. Having mounted, having performed the rite of the northern altar-fire (*auttaravedika*), he should take the fire into himself.
Having taken the fire into himself, he sings the *satya-sāman* and lays down a lotus leaf. From that [it proceeds]. 7.3.2. [18]

Then, when evening has come, they lead this horse around. For the gods were afraid of this, thinking, "Lest the *rakṣases*, the destroyers, should slay him here"; therefore, for his sake, they [lead it].
They made that very sun the protector of the thunderbolt; for yonder sun is this horse, and so he makes him the protector of this thunderbolt for him.
He leads it around until the setting of the sun.

Verily, this [fire] becomes his manifest protector by day, while the Rakṣases are indeed the companions of the night; thus he makes this thunderbolt his protector during the night. He carries it around on all sides;
verily, he makes this thunderbolt his protector on every side. He carries it around three times.

He makes this threefold thunderbolt his protector; then he sends it forth toward the north and the east—the significance of that has been explained—and then it turns back again, the significance of which is explained above. 7.4.1.
When about to perform the piling, he takes the fire into himself.
For he generates this very self from his own self; as one is born from what [he is], so indeed does he become.

If he were to pile the fire-altar without having taken it into himself, he would generate a human from a human, a mortal from a mortal, one whose evil has not been struck away from one whose evil has not been struck away. But then—

When he takes the fire into himself and piles it up, he thereby produces from Agni itself another Agni—immortality from immortality, one whose evil has been struck away from one whose evil has been struck away. 7.4.1.
[2] He takes it up with the formula: "In me I first take Agni. Thus he first takes Agni into himself for the sake of the increase of wealth.

With the words, "For good offspring, for great heroism," he thus takes all blessings into himself; with the words, "May the deities attend upon me," he thus takes all the gods into himself. Whatever he is about to produce from himself, he takes all that into himself.
Having taken Agni into himself while standing, he then sits down and builds him up.
This Agni is an animal; therefore, an animal, having conceived while standing, gives birth after sitting down. 7.4.1 [3] Then he sings the Satya Sāman.
For the gods said, "Let us make truth its mouth."
"Truly we shall become; truth will follow us; that desire of ours shall become true, which desire we shall fulfill by doing this.
Thus they sang this *sāman* of truth in the beginning.
They made that his true face;
they became Truth, and Truth followed after them. That desire of theirs became Truth, which was the desire with which they performed this rite. 7.4.1 [5]
In the same way, this sacrificer:
when he sings the *sāman* of truth in front, he makes truth his mouth;
he becomes truth, truth follows him, and whatever desire he has, that desire of his becomes true.
It performs this [action]. 7.4.1.[6] That which is the Truth (satya) is indeed water; for water is indeed the Truth. Therefore, wherever water flows, that is the path of the Truth.

"They say that 'form' is indeed water; they made it the beginning of all this. Therefore, whenever the waters flow, then all this is born—whatever there is here. 7.4.1. [7] Now he lays down a lotus leaf.
The lotus leaf is indeed the womb; it is the womb that he thus lays down. Furthermore, as to why he lays down the lotus leaf:
the lotus is the waters, and this [earth] is their leaf (parṇa). Just as...
Or rather, this lotus leaf was placed upon the waters; even so, this [earth] is placed upon the waters. This is the womb of Agni, for this is Agni, since the whole of Agni is built upon her.

It is this very [earth] that he thus lays down. He lays it down not separated from the *satya* (truth); he thereby establishes this [earth] upon the *satya*. Therefore, this [earth] rests upon the *satya*.
Therefore, this [earth] alone is established as the truth, for she is the most manifest of these worlds. 7.4.1.
"Thou art the back of the waters, the womb of Agni. For she is indeed the back of the waters, and she is the womb of Agni.
"Swelling on all sides toward the ocean"—the ocean swells toward the oblations as he grows;

"growing great upon the lotus"—that is, "grow greater upon the lotus"; "spread out by the measure and breadth of heaven"—he strokes [it] along; for yonder sun is this very Agni, and there is no other breadth than that of heaven.
"He ought to restrain him; having become the sky, he shall restrain him"—this is what he says by this. He lays it down with the *svarāj* formula, for he is a self-ruler (*svarāj*).
Having settled it with the *sūdadohas* verse, he recites over it the *sūdadohas*; the significance of that has already been explained.
7.4.1. [10] Now he lays down the gold plate (*rukma*).

Yonder sun, indeed, is this gold plate; for he outshines all these creatures. "Roca" (the shining one), they cryptically call him "rukbha" (gold plate); for the gods love the cryptic. It is yonder sun that he thus lays down. It is made of gold and is circular.
Its twenty-one *nirbādhas* have been declared; he places the *nirbādha* below it, for these *nirbādhas* are indeed its rays, and its rays are below it.
He places it upon a lotus leaf.
The lotus leaf is indeed the womb; he thus establishes him in the womb. Furthermore, as to why he lays down a lotus leaf.
The lotus leaf is indeed a foundation; this earth is the lotus leaf, for this earth is the foundation. Whoever is not established upon it, even if he is far away, is indeed without a foundation.
But by means of its rays, this [sun] is established upon this [earth].
He thus establishes him in this very foundation.
Furthermore, as to why he places it on a lotus leaf:
having slain Vṛtra, Indra, thinking "I have not struck him down," [entered] the waters.

He entered it and said, "I am indeed afraid; prepare a fortress for me. They gathered together the essence of the waters that was there and built a fortress for him. Because they built a fortress (*pura*) for him, it is called *pūṣkara*.
Indeed, they call it *puṣkara* cryptically, for people desire the cryptic.

The gods, when they placed that lotus leaf (puṣkaraparṇa) upon it, established him in that very place where the waters had gathered his essence and fashioned for him a fortress. "Brahman, born first in the east... [he says]. 7.4.1. [14]

Yonder sun, indeed, is the Brahman; day after day it is born in the east. "Vena has disclosed [the world] from the bright boundary" (RV 7.89.5). The "boundary" (*sīman*) is the middle, and these worlds are the "bright ones" (*surucaḥ*);
yonder sun is Vena. Because he looked down (*avekṣata*) while about to be born, therefore he is called Vena; him, from that boundary, from the middle, this one [the sun] [discloses].

"Raining down, he rises; his highest stations are the depths. The quarters, indeed, are his highest stations, for it is toward them that he spreads out. "The womb of both the existent and the non-existent"—these worlds are indeed the womb of both the existent and the non-existent, for whatever exists and whatever does not exist, all that is born from these very worlds. He lays it down with a *triṣṭubh* verse.
For this [verse] belongs to the Triṣṭubh; having settled it, he recites over it the *sūdadohas* verse; its significance has already been explained.
7.4.1. [15] Then he lays down a man.
He is Prajāpati, he is Agni, he is the sacrificer; he is made of gold.
Gold is indeed light, and Agni is light; gold is immortality, and Agni is immortality. He becomes a person (puruṣa), for Prajāpati is indeed a person.
Furthermore, as to why he lays down a person.
From Prajāpati, when he had become relaxed, his beautiful body emerged from the middle.
When that [body] had departed from him, the gods abandoned him.
Where the gods restored him, there they placed this beautiful body back into him from the middle; in it, the gods [re-established] him.

The gods took delight in that very delightful body of his; because they took delight (aramanta) therein, it is called *hiranya*. Indeed, they call it *hiranya* cryptically (*parokṣam*), for the gods love the cryptic. In the same way, he now places this delightful body in the middle of him. In it, the gods [dwell].
They delight; for the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is indeed his delightful body. He thus places this very vital breath in the middle of him. 7.4.1. [17] He lays down that gold plate (*rukma*).
Yonder sun is indeed this gold plate; and now, he who is in this orb—
This is that very Puruṣa; it is him that he thus lays down.
He lays it down face upwards.
For the gods said, "If we were to lay these two face downwards," [they would be turned away from us].
"If both of these face away, they will burn everything here;
if they face together, these two will scorch each other, and this light will disappear between them, and furthermore, they will harm one another.
Thinking thus, they placed one facing toward them and the other facing away. This is that gold plate (rukma) which shines toward us with its rays.
With the vital breaths, he lays down this Puruṣa facing eastward, for this Agni is piled facing the east.
"Hiraṇyagarbha arose in the beginning"—
for he, as Hiraṇyagarbha, arose in the beginning of all that exists.

"Once born, he was the sole lord"—for he, once born, was indeed the sole lord of all this being; "he supported the earth and this heaven"—for he indeed supported both heaven and earth; "to what god shall we offer worship with oblation?"—Prajāpati is indeed "Ka"; thus, "to him let us offer worship with oblation. 7.4.1 [20]
"The drop has fallen upon the earth and across the sky"—the drop is indeed that Āditya; he falls upon both heaven and earth.
"Upon that [one] and upon this one, upon this womb and that which was before"—[he falls] upon this world and that one.

And this which is now being piled, and that which was piled here before—[the verse says] "moving along toward a common womb," for he indeed moves along toward this same womb; "I offer the drop according to the seven Hotṛ-offices"—that drop is indeed yonder sun, and the seven Hotṛ-offices are the quarters; he thus places yonder sun in the quarters.
He establishes it. He lays down two [bricks];
the sacrificer is two-footed, and the sacrificer is Agni. As great as Agni is, as great as is his measure—
He lays it down with just that much; he does so with two Triṣṭubh verses, for this [brick] is of the Triṣṭubh nature.
Having settled it, he pronounces the Sūdadohas verse over it; the significance of that has already been explained. Then he sings a Sāman.
The gods, having laid down this person, saw him exactly as he was—just like this dry plank.
They said, "Find out how we may place vigor into this person. Thus they spoke.
When they said, "Meditate! (*cetayadhvam*), they were indeed saying, "Seek the layer" (*citim icata*).
They sought it [thinking], "Let us place vigor (*vīrya*) in this person. 7.4.1. [24] While they were thus meditating...
They saw this *sāman* and sang it; they placed vigor (*vīrya*) within it. In the same way, this [priest] now places that [vigor] within him.

He sings for the *puruṣa*; he thus places vigor in the *puruṣa*. He sings for the *citra*; for Agni is all wonders (*citra*). Having laid down that [brick], one should not pass around its front, lest this Agni injure me. 7.4.1. [25]
Then he worships with the names of the serpents.
These worlds, indeed, are the serpents; they glide along by means of this entire [world]—whatever there is here. This Agni is indeed the self of all these gods; those gods...

Having placed this self within themselves, they were afraid, thinking, "Lest these worlds, through this self, should not reach us. They saw these names of serpents; with them they approached [the world], and by them they reached it. 7.4.1 [26]
He established these worlds and made them firm with those [names]; because he made them firm (*anamayan*), therefore they are called "Sarpa-names" (snakes).

In the same way, when the sacrificer worships with the Sarpa-names, he establishes these very worlds for him and makes these worlds firm. Thus, by means of this self, they do not crawl over him. 7.4.1. [27]
Furthermore, as to why he worships with the names of serpents:

these worlds are indeed the serpents, for whatever creeps (sarpati) does so within these very worlds. Thus, when he worships with the names of serpents, it is to drive away whatever destructive power (nāṣṭrā) exists in these worlds.
Whatever is harmful and whatever is injurious—all that he pacifies.
Homage be to the serpents, whichever ones are upon the earth, those who are in the intermediate space, and those who are in heaven; to those serpents [be homage].
"Obeisance!"—he thus pays homage to those serpents that are in these three worlds.
"The arrows of the sorcerers"—some say these are those sent by sorcerers who bite, or those that dwell in the trees. 7.4.1 [29]

"To those serpents who lie in holes, homage!"—by saying this, he pays homage to those serpents who are in the trees and those who lie in holes. "Those who are in the bright realm of heaven... 7.4.1 [30]

"Or those who are in the rays of the sun, or those whose seat is made in the waters—to those serpents, homage! Wherever they may be, it is to them that he thus pays homage. "Homage, homage!"—homage is indeed the sacrifice;
by means of the sacrifice, he thus pays homage to them with this act of homage. Therefore, one should not [use] what is unsacrificial.
He should say, "Salutation to you. This is just as if one were to say to him, "Sacrifice to you"; such is that. He worships with three [verses].
These worlds are three; moreover, Agni is threefold. As great as Agni is, as great as is his measure—so much is this.
By that much alone he establishes these worlds for him; moreover, by that much alone he pacifies all this.
He stands while performing the *upasthāna*, for these worlds are, as it were, standing; furthermore, one who stands is indeed more powerful. Then, having sat down, he makes offerings over it.
With ghee taken in five ladlings—the significance of this has been explained—he moves around it on all sides;
thus he gratifies it with food from all directions.
And as to why he offers over it:

The gods, having laid down this self (ātman), were afraid, thinking, "Lest the Rakṣases, the destroyers, should slay us here. They saw these Rakṣas-slaying *pratisaras* (protective charms), beginning with, "Make thy strength wide like a snare" (*kṛṇuṣva pājaḥ prasitiṃ na pṛthvīm*). These *pratisaras* are indeed Rakṣas-slayers; by means of these *pratisaras*, from all [directions]...
Having driven away the Rakṣases and destroyers from all directions, they fashioned this self in a state free from danger and destruction;

in the same way, the sacrificer now, by means of these amulets, drives away the Rakṣases and destroyers from all directions and fashions this self in a state free from danger and destruction. 7.4.1 [34]
He offers with clarified butter;
for clarified butter is indeed a thunderbolt, and by means of that thunderbolt he strikes away the destructive spirits. He offers with [butter] taken five times;
for the fire-altar consists of five layers, there are five seasons in the year, and the year is Agni—as great as Agni is, as great as his measure is...
By that much alone he repels the *rakṣas* and the destroyers;
with verses addressed to Agni—for Agni is light, the slayer of *rakṣas*—he thereby repels the *rakṣas* and the destroyers.
With *triṣṭubh* verses—for the *triṣṭubh* is indeed the thunderbolt—he thereby repels the *rakṣas* and the destroyers by means of the thunderbolt. [He does so] by crawling all around on every side.
In this way, he drives away the *rakṣas* and the destroyers from all directions:
first, sitting behind the fire facing east; then from the north facing south; then from the front facing west; and then along the rear.
Having gone around by the right and sitting facing north, he places it; for that is turned toward the south, for so it is among the gods.
Then, having gone around again and sitting behind facing east, his work is thus performed from the very beginning. 7.4.1.
[36] Now he lays down two offering-spoons (sruc).

The two arms are indeed the two offering-spoons; he thus restores the two arms to him. As to why they are two spoons: the two arms are indeed two spoons. This [upper part] is the bowl and this [lower part] is the handle; there are two of them, for these two arms are two. He places them on the sides, for these two arms are on the sides. 7.4.1 [37]
He places one made of *kārṣmarya* wood to the south.
For the gods were indeed afraid, thinking, "Lest the Rakṣases, the destroyers, should strike our sacrifice from the south"; they [therefore] prepared this slayer of Rakṣases.

They saw the *kārṣmarya* tree as a lord of the forest; with this lord of the forest, having driven away the destructive *rakṣases* from the south, they performed this sacrifice in a place free from danger and destruction. In the same way, the sacrificer now, having driven away the destructive *rakṣases* from the south by means of this lord of the forest, performs this sacrifice in a place free from danger and destruction. [The ladle] is filled with clarified butter.
The *vajra* is indeed clarified butter (*ājya*); by means of the *vajra*, he thus repels the obstructing demons (*rakṣas*) from the south.
Then he places a block of *udumbara* wood to the north;
the *udumbara* is strength and sap; verily, he thereby bestows strength and sap upon this [fire-altar].
He places [the brick]; it is filled with curds. Curds are indeed essence; he thus bestows essence upon this [Agni]. 7.4.1.
[39] Furthermore, as to why he places two offering-spoons (sruc):
when Prajāpati had become relaxed, Agni took his fiery luster (tejas) and drew it away toward the south. So...
He dug up its root and ate it; therefore it is the *kārṣmarya*. Then Indra, having taken away its vital strength (*ojas*), departed toward the north, and it became the *udumbara* tree.
He said to those two:
"Come here! Give this back to me by which you two have departed from me!
"Then give us all food! "In that case, enter me as my two arms!
"So be it. He gave them all the food; they both entered him, having become his two arms.
Therefore, food is prepared by the two arms alone; it is eaten by the two arms; for with his two arms he bestowed all that food.
7.4.1.[41] He places one made of *kārṣmarya* wood to the south.

With the words, "O Agni, I settle thee with thy brilliance," he restores to him that very brilliance which Agni had taken away and drawn toward the south; [he does so] with the verse, "Agni is the head, the summit of heaven," for this indeed is that Agni; it is with a Gāyatrī verse, because Agni is of the Gāyatrī nature—so great as is Agni, so great is his measure.
It is for this very reason that he lays it down; it is full of clarified butter (*ghṛta*). Clarified butter indeed belongs to Agni;
thus he gratifies him with his own portion, with his own delight.
Then he lays down a block of Udumbara wood to the north.

With the words, "By Indra's might I set thee down," he takes up that very might of his, Indra, and having taken it, he steps out toward the north; with this [verse] he restores it to him. With the words, "Thou art the leader of the sacrifice and of the region," for he is indeed that Indra. As for its being addressed to Agni, it is because it pertains to a rite for Agni; and as for its being a Triṣṭubh, it is because Indra is of the nature of the Triṣṭubh.

The fire-altar belongs to Indra and Agni; as great as the fire is, as great as its measure is, with just that much he thus lays it down. Indeed, Indra and Agni are all the gods, and the fire-altar belongs to all the deities; as great as the fire is, as great as its measure is, with just that much he thus lays it down. It is filled with curds; for curds belong to Indra.
He thus gratifies him with his own portion, with his own essence.
Those two, Indra and Agni, are indeed his two arms; they approach him together with splendor and vigor. He...
Now, having made the man visible on the chest, he draws that upon which he reaches and lays those [bricks] down;
for this indeed is the world of these two. Some, however, lay them down crosswise.
"These two arms are indeed horizontal," they say; one should not do so.

One should lay them down facing eastward, for this Agni is built facing the east. Moreover, in this way the two arms are more powerful. He lays them down separately, settles them separately, and pronounces the *sūdadohas* verse over them separately, for these two arms are separate. 7.4.1 [45]
Regarding this they say: "One should not make arms for this person, for these two spoons (*srucau*) are his arms; one must not make them redundant.
Yet, he should indeed make them; for these two spoons follow after these two arms of his, and furthermore, they are his wings.
Moreover, whatever forms (*rūpa*), whatever *stomas*, and whatever *pṛṣṭhas* he is about to place upon this fire-altar—[all these are contained therein].
Whatever *candāṃsi* there are, they are the refinement of these two, the growth of these two; therefore, one should indeed fashion the two arms of this person.
He lays down the *svayamātṛṇṇā* brick.
This is indeed the *svayamātṛṇā* (self-perforated brick); it is this very [earth] that he thus lays down. He lays it down so as not to be separated from the man. The *svayamātṛṇā* is food;
this earth is the *svayamātṛṇā*, for this earth is food, since all food is cooked upon it.
Verily, he places this food for him without interruption; he places this food for him ever higher and higher.
Furthermore, as to why he lays down the *svayamātṛṇṇā* brick:
the *svayamātṛṇṇā* is indeed breath; it is breath.

Verily, he thus cuts out for himself from his own self; he lays down this very vital breath (prāṇa). He lays it down so as not to be separated from the person. For the naturally perforated brick (svayamātṛṇā) is indeed the vital breath; this earth is the naturally perforated brick, and this earth is the vital breath. For whatever is possessed of breath, all that she sustains; thus, he places the vital breath so as not to be separated from him.
He places it higher and higher; verily, he thus bestows vital breath upon him from above. Furthermore, as for why he lays down the *svayamātṛṇṇā* brick:
when Prajāpati had become disjointed, the deities took him up.
As they were stepping out, he stepped out after them; having reached a firm foundation, he sat down.
That Prajāpati who fell apart is this very Agni who is now being built up; and that which was she—

This is the foundation; it is the first *svayamātṛṇṇā* brick. In that he lays this one here, he thereby restores to him that which belongs to this [altar's] self; therefore, he lays this one here. He indeed lays it down with Prajāpati.
For Prajāpati himself placed this upon himself.
"Thou art firm" means "thou art steady," and also "thou art established. "Support" (*dharuṇa*): the support is indeed a foundation;
"spread by Viśvakarman"—Prajāpati is indeed Viśvakarman—therefore it means "by him thou art spread. "May the ocean not [overwhelm] thee..."
"May the fair-winged one not strike thee down"—the fair-winged one is indeed the man, and the fire-plate is the ocean; thus, "may those two not strike thee down.
"Without trembling, do thou steady the earth"—as the sacrificial formula is, so is its significance.
"May Prajāpati settle thee."

For Prajāpati saw this first layer: "On the back of the waters, on the seat of the ocean. For this is indeed the back of the waters, and this is the seat of the ocean. "Spacious, wide-extending"—for it is indeed spacious and wide-extending. "Spread out, O Earth, thou art"—spread out!
"Pṛthivī cāsi" (And you are the earth) [is the same as] "bhūrasi.
For this [earth] is indeed *bhūḥ*. "Bhūmirasi" means "you are the earth," for this is indeed the earth. "Aditirasi" means "you are Aditi," for this [earth] is indeed Aditi;
she gives (*dadate*) all this. "Viśvadhāyāḥ" means "in whom all this is placed (*hitam*). "Dhartrī viśvasya bhuvanasya" means "the upholder of the entire world."
"Supporter of the entire world"—this refers to the earth; "stabilize the earth, do not harm the earth"—this refers to oneself; "stabilize yourself, do not harm yourself"—this is what it means.
For the sake of every out-breath and in-breath.

"For the diffused breath (vyāna), for the upward breath (udāna)!"—the naturally perforated brick is indeed the vital breath (prāṇa), and the vital breath serves as a support for all this; "for stability, for movement"—these worlds are indeed the naturally perforated bricks, and these worlds are stability and movement. "May Agni protect you"—that is, "may Agni guard you"; "with great well-being."

With the words "Great well-being," he means "with the most peaceful roof. Having settled it, he pronounces the *sūdadohas* verse; its significance has already been explained. Then he sings the *Sāman*; its significance follows later. Regarding this they say: "How is it that this person is not pierced by the *svayamātṛṇā* brick? It is food indeed.
The *svayamātṛṇā* brick is the vital breath; for a person is indeed established by means of both food and the vital breath. Then he lays down the *dūrveṣṭakā* brick.
The *dūrveṣṭakā* is cattle; it is cattle that he thus lays down.

Now, with those very animals that Agni approached without any interval, he now places these [bricks]; he places them without any interval from the *svayamātṛṇā* brick. This earth, indeed, is the *svayamātṛṇā*; thus he places the animals within her.
He places each subsequent one higher than the last; thus he places the animals higher and higher within her. 7.4.2. [11]
Furthermore, as to why he lays down a *dūrveṣṭakā* brick:
when Prajāpati had become relaxed, those hairs of his that fell away became these plants; then, the vital breath (*prāṇa*) departed from his center, and when it had departed, he fell down. 7.4.2 [12]
He said: "Verily, this one has not crushed me (mā adhūrvīt)," because he said, "Do not crush me (mā adhūrvīḥ)," therefore it is *dhūrvā*.
They call it *dūrvā* cryptically, for the gods love the cryptic. This is the ruling power (*kṣatra*), for it is breath;
it is sap, while the other plants are the hair. By laying down this brick, he lays down all plants. 7.4.2.13.

Where the gods restored him, they placed this vital breath (*prāṇa*), this essence, in the middle of him; in the very same way, he now places it in him. He places it immediately adjacent to the *svayamātṛṇṇā* brick.

He lays them down. This earth is indeed the *svayamātṛṇā*; he thus places plants upon her. He places them one after another; he thus places plants upon her one after another. They should have roots and tips for the sake of completeness.
He should lay them down in such a way that they reach the ground once placed upon the *svayamātṛṇā*, for it is upon this very [earth] that these [plants] [are established].
They are born following this [earth] and they grow forth. "From joint to joint she grows forth, from node to node," for indeed, she grows from joint to joint.
"From joint to joint it indeed grows for us; extend us further by a thousand and a hundred"—as the sacrificial formula (*yajus*) is, so is its significance (*bandhu*).
"She who extends with a hundred... [7.4.2.15]
"With a thousand you grow forth"—for she spreads with a hundred and grows forth with a thousand;
"to you, O divine brick, we shall pay worship with an oblation"—as the sacrificial formula (yajus) is, so is its significance (bandhu).
With two [formulas] he lays it down; its significance has been explained. Having settled it, he pronounces the *sūdadohas* verse over it.
Its connection has been stated [in the preceding section]. 7.4.2.
[16] Now he lays down the two-brick formula (*dviyajus*):
Indra and Agni desired, "May we go to the heavenly world."

The two of them saw this brick, the Dviyajuḥ; they placed it here. Having placed it, they went from this foundation to the heavenly world. In the same way, when the sacrificer places the Dviyajuḥ brick, he does so by means of that form and having performed that action by which Indra and Agni went to the heavenly world, he goes [to the heavenly world] by that same form and having performed that same action.
"I am leading him to the heavenly world. As for that which is called *dviyajuḥ*, it is because two deities saw this [brick];

and furthermore, as to why he lays down the *dviyajuḥ* brick—the *dviyajuḥ* is indeed the sacrificer. Regarding this, they say: "Since that very sacrificer is this golden person (*hiraṇmaya-puruṣa*), then what is this [brick] of his?"
"Form"—this is his divine self, while this [other form] is his human self. In that he is made of gold, that is his immortal form, the divine form;
for gold is immortality. And in that this [other form] is made of clay, that is his human form, for this [clay] is indeed human. 7.4.2. [18]
If he were to lay down only that [upper layer] and were not to leave this [lower layer] remaining, the sacrificer would quickly depart from this world;
but in that he leaves this one remaining, he thereby leaves behind that which is his human form.
For thus, by means of this self, he attains his full lifespan.
If he were not to place these [bricks] alongside, he would not come to know this divine self; therefore, he places them alongside.

In this way, he understands that divine Self. He places it immediately adjacent to the *dūrvā*-brick; for the *dūrvā*-brick is indeed cattle. Thus, he establishes the sacrificer in cattle. 7.4.2. Regarding this they say: "How do these two bodies of his become continuous and uninterrupted by means of the vital breath (*prāṇa*)? It is the vital breath, indeed...

The *svayamātṛṇā* is the breath; the *dūrveṣṭakā* is the sacrificer, the *dviyajuṣ*. When he places the *dūrveṣṭakā* not separated from the *svayamātṛṇā*, he thereby extends and joins the breath with the breath.
And when he places the *dviyajuṣ* not separated from the *dūrveṣṭakā*, the *dūrveṣṭakā* is indeed the breath.
The sacrificer is indeed a *dviyajuṣ*. Thus, these two bodies of his become continuous and uninterrupted by means of the vital breath (*prāṇa*).

"O Agni, those splendors (*rucaḥ*) of yours which are in the sun; O gods, those splendors of yours which are in the sun"—by saying "splendor, splendor" (*rucam rucam*), he [attains] immortality. Indeed, splendor is immortality.
He bestows upon this [brick] both disease and immortality; he lays it down with two verses, the significance of which has been explained.
Moreover, this form consists of a dyad, namely clay and water. Having settled it, he pronounces the *sūdadohas* verse over it, the significance of which has also been explained.
7.4.2. Then he lays down the two *retaḥsic* bricks.
These two worlds, indeed, are the two semen-shedders (retaḥsic), for these two worlds shed semen from here. This [world] sheds semen upwards as smoke; there it becomes rain.
From that rain, those [beings] are produced between these two worlds. Therefore, these two worlds are the two semen-shedders. 7.4.2. [23]
"Virāj has sustained the light"—this world is indeed Virāj; it sustains this Agni as the light.
"Svarāj has sustained the light"—that world is indeed Svarāj; it sustains yonder sun as the light.
The Virāj and the Svarāj are these two worlds; he lays them down separately, for separate indeed are these two worlds. He settles them once, thereby making them common;
therefore, the ends of these two worlds meet together.
Furthermore, as to why he lays down the two Retahsic bricks.
The two testicles are indeed the two seed-shedders; for he who has testicles is the one who sheds seed.

"The Virāj held the light; the Svarāj held the light"—for these two testicles are the Virāj and the Svarāj, and they both hold this light, namely the seed, namely Prajāpati. He lays them down separately, separately.
He places the two *homa*-bricks together once; he thus makes them uniform, and therefore they are connected as a pair.
He lays down the two *dviyajus* bricks without an interval; the *dviyajus* is indeed the sacrificer; he thus places the two testicles in immediate proximity to the sacrificer. 7.4.2. [25]
Then he lays down the Viśvajyotis brick.
Agni indeed is the first Viśvajyotis, for Agni alone is the all-light in this world;
it is Agni whom he thus lays down. He lays it down immediately adjacent to the two Retahsic bricks, [representing] these two worlds.
Verily, these two worlds are the two semen-shedders; he thus places Agni between these two worlds.
He places it within, for Agni is indeed within these two worlds.
Furthermore, as to why he lays down the Viśvajyotis brick.
Offspring, indeed, is the Viśvajyotis, for offspring is indeed the universal light;
he thus lays down this [brick] as procreation. He lays it down so as not to be separated from the two Retahsic bricks; for the two Retahsic are the testicles;
he thus places procreation within the testicles. He lays it down right in between, indeed within.
"From the two testicles, offspring are produced.
"May Prajāpati settle you"—
for Prajāpati perceived this first layer upon the back of the earth.

"Jyotiṣmatīm" (the luminous one)—for on the back of the earth this Agni is indeed luminous. "For all out-breathing, in-breathing, and diffused breathing"—for the Viśvajyotis is indeed the breath; it is for all this that breath [is offered].

"Thou art the light of the universe"—that is, "thou art all the light. "Agni is thy overlord"—he thus makes Agni the overlord of this [brick]. Having settled it, he pronounces the *sūdadohas* verse; its significance has already been explained. 7.4.2.
Then he lays down the two seasonal bricks (*ṛtavyā*).
These two seasonal bricks are the seasons; it is thus the seasons he lays down. "Madhu and Mādhava, the two spring seasons"—these are their names; it is by these very names that he lays them down.
There are two bricks, for a season consists of two months. He settles them once; he thereby makes it one season. 7.4.2. [30]
Now, as to why he lays these down here:
this Agni is the year, and the year is these worlds.
Of that [year], this world is the first layer; of this world, the spring season is [the first layer]. Therefore, when he lays these down here, it is because they belong to this [world] of his.
He thus places that [part] of himself into this; therefore he lays these two down here.
Furthermore, as to why he lays these two down here:
this Agni is Prajāpati, and Prajāpati is the year; of him—

The first layer is indeed the foundation; the spring season is his foundation. Therefore, when he places these two bricks here, he restores to him that which belongs to this body of his; that is why he places these two here.
He places them immediately adjacent to the *viśvajyotis* bricks. The *viśvajyotis* (all-light) bricks are indeed offspring; thus, he places offspring immediately adjacent to the seasons.

He places it; therefore offspring are born according to the seasons, for they perceive him while he is still in the womb by means of the seasons, and they perceive him when he is born by means of the seasons. 7.4.2.
[32] Then he lays down the Ashāḍhā brick.
This indeed is the Aṣāḍhā; he thus lays down this very one. He lays it down in the eastern half, for this was the first to be created.
As for why it is named Aṣāḍhā:
The gods and the Asuras, both offspring of Prajāpati, contended with one another. The gods perceived this *iṣṭakā*, namely this very *aṣāḍhā*; they laid it down.
Having laid it down, they overcame their rivals, their enemies, the Asuras, from all this [universe]. Because they overcame (*asahanta*) them...
Therefore, by laying down this Aṣāḍhā brick in the same manner, the sacrificer overcomes his hateful rival from all this [universe]. Furthermore, as to why he lays down the Aṣāḍhā.

The Aṣāḍhā is indeed speech; by means of speech, the gods then overcame the Asuras—their rivals and enemies—from out of this entire world. In the same way, the sacrificer now overcomes his hateful rival from out of this entire world by means of speech alone. It was speech that the gods thus established.
In the same way, the sacrificer thereby lays down speech itself.
This [earth] is the *vāmabhṛt*. The breaths are indeed the desirable (*vāma*); for whatever is possessed of breath, this [earth] supports it all; therefore she is [called] this.
The Vāmabhṛt is indeed speech; for the desirable (vāma) is the vital breaths, and in speech the food is placed for the sake of the vital breaths;
therefore, speech is the Vāmabhṛt. All these vital breaths are the Aṣāḍhā.
He places it on the eastern half; he thereby places the vital breaths (prāṇas) in the front.

Therefore, these vital breaths are in the front. He should not place it in front with any other brick possessing a sacrificial formula (yajuṣmatī), lest he should enclose the vital breaths within this layer (citi). 7.4.2. [37]
As for why he places five *vapā* bricks in front:

the waters are indeed food, and the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) are not covered over by food. He places them immediately adjacent to the two seasonal bricks; thus, he establishes speech within the seasons. This [speech] is...
Speech, established in the seasons, speaks.
Regarding this they say: "Since the *viśvajyotis* bricks are offspring and the *aṣāḍhā* is speech, why does he place the two seasonal (*ṛtavyā*) bricks between them?
The two seasonal bricks are indeed the year; thus, by means of the year, he interposes speech for the sake of offspring.
Therefore, at the time of the year, creatures utter speech: "Thou art the invincible, the overcoming one. For by her the gods overcame the Asuras; overcome the enemies, overcome those who attack!

Thus, as the *yajus* is, so is its significance: "Thou art of thousandfold power; do thou quicken me. A thousand is indeed everything; thus it means, "Thou art of all-power; do thou quicken me. Having settled it, he pronounces the *sūdadohas* verse over it; the significance of that has already been explained. Regarding this they say: "Why are the other bricks laid down facing toward the *svayamātṛṇā*, while these [the *svayamātṛṇās*] are laid down facing eastward? There are two [answers].

"One should say they are 'wombs' (yonī). One is the womb of the gods, the other is the womb of men. The gods indeed have their procreation facing eastward, while men have their procreation facing westward. Therefore, when he lays these down facing eastward, he causes the sacrificer to be born from the womb of the gods. 7.5.1.1.
He places the tortoise.
The tortoise is indeed the essence; it is the essence that he thus places.
That essence of these worlds which, when they were cast into the waters, flowed away—this is that very tortoise; it is him that he thus places.
As great as the essence is, so great is the Self; that very Self is these worlds.
Of that [Self], the lower skull is this world, and it is, as it were, firmly established, for this world is, as it were, firmly established.

This [lower part] is this world, and that which is above is the sky; it has its ends as if held apart, for the sky has its ends as if held apart. And what is between them is the intermediate space. This very thing is these worlds;
he thus lays down these very worlds. 7.5.1. [3]

He anoints him with curds, honey, and ghee; for curds are the form of this world, ghee is the form of the intermediate space, and honey is the form of yonder world; he thus endows him with his own respective forms. Moreover—
Curd is indeed the essence of this world, ghee of the intermediate space, and honey of yonder world; by means of its own essence, he thus causes him to prosper.
"The winds blow honey for the one who follows the cosmic order," [he says].

Whatever deity a *ṛc* verse refers to, and whatever deity a *yajus* formula refers to, that indeed is the deity; this [verse] has the eye as its deity and this [formula] has the eye as its *yajus*. This very three-verse hymn (*ṛca*) is honey;
honey is essence. Thus, he places essence into him. It consists of three *gāyatrī* verses; the significance of this has already been explained. 7.5.1. [5]
As for that which is called the tortoise:
having assumed this very form, Prajāpati created the creatures.
Because he created—that is, because he made (akarot)—therefore it is called a tortoise (kūrma). Kaśyapa is indeed the tortoise; therefore they say [of him], "all."
"O descendants of Kaśyapa, [these are] the subjects.
7.5.1.[6] That which is the tortoise is this very Āditya; it is this Āditya whom he thus lays down. Him—

He places it facing westward from the east; he thus places yonder sun facing westward from the east, and therefore yonder sun is placed facing westward from the east. To the south of the Aṣāḍhā brick he places it;
for the tortoise is a male and the Aṣāḍhā is a female, and the male lies to the south of the female at a distance of one cubit, for the male is [placed] at a distance of one cubit.
He lies beside the woman; she is the queen (*mahiṣī*) of all the bricks, namely this *aṣāḍhā*.
Being to its south, it comes to be to the south of all the bricks.
And as to why he places the tortoise there...

The tortoise is indeed the vital breath (*prāṇa*), for the vital breath creates all these creatures; it is the vital breath that he thus lays down. He places it facing westward from the east; verily, he thereby places the vital breath facing westward from the east.
Therefore, the vital breath is placed facing westward from the east, directed toward the person, upon the sacrificer.
He places that vital breath to the south of the Aṣāḍhā brick. The tortoise is indeed the vital breath, and the Aṣāḍhā is speech;
the vital breath is the male of speech, and the vital breath is the couple.
"He should step upon the depths of the waters," [he says].
"This indeed is the deepest part of the waters, where this one [the sun] now shines;

may the sun not scorch you, nor Agni Vaiśvānara!"—this means "May the sun not harm you, nor Agni Vaiśvānara. "O thou with unbroken wings, look upon the offspring"—these indeed are all the offspring that these bricks are; they are unhurt.
"Look around without distress"— by saying "may the divine rain attend you," he speaks thus so that the divine rain may indeed attend him.
7.5.1 [9] Then he makes it move.

"He has glided across the three oceans, the heavens"—these indeed are the three oceans, the heavenly worlds; having become a tortoise, he has glided along them. "The lord of the waters, the bull of the bricks"—for he is indeed the lord of the waters, the bull of the bricks. "Clothed in soil, in the world of the well-made"—the soil is indeed cattle.

"Clad in cattle in the world of the well-done"—this means "go there where the ancients have departed," that is, "go there where the ancients went by this rite. "May the great heaven and earth [protect us]"—[so it is said].* *Note: The final phrase is the beginning of the next verse (RV 1.22.13) which continues with "be favorable to us."*

"May the great heaven and earth for us"—this means "may they mix this sacrifice"; "may they protect this sacrifice"—this means "may they favor this sacrifice"; "may they sustain us with nourishments"—this means "may they support us with nourishments. He places [the brick] with the last verse concerning heaven and earth, for the tortoise is indeed heaven and earth. 7.5.1. [11]
He lays down three;

these worlds are three, and Agni is threefold. As great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, with just that much he thus lays him down. He anoints them with three [verses]; that makes six; the significance of that has been explained. Avakā plants...
Below are the *avakā* plants and above are the waters—or rather, the *avakās* are themselves water; he thus places him in the midst of the waters.
Having settled it, he pronounces the *sūdadohas* verse over it; its significance has already been explained.
Then he lays down the mortar and pestle.
Viṣṇu desired, "May I be an eater of food.

He saw these two bricks, the mortar and the pestle; he laid them down, and having laid them down, he became an eater of food. In the same way, when the sacrificer lays down the mortar and the pestle, it is by that very form and by performing that same rite that Viṣṇu became an eater of food.

Having performed that rite with its outward form, thinking, "May I be an eater of food," he places it there; for all this is food—since it is by means of the mortar and pestle that food is prepared, and it is by means of the mortar and pestle that it is eaten.
He places them on the level of the two *retahsic* bricks.
The two *pṛṣṭhas* are the two semen-shedders (*retaḥsic*), and the *pṛṣṭhas* are the middle;
thus he places this food in him from the very middle. They are on the higher [side]; he thus places this food for him at the higher [level]. At the distance of an *aratni* (cubit);
for food is eaten at the distance of an *aratni*. 7.5.1. [14]
They are a span in measure.
For Viṣṇu, the embryo, is indeed a span in measure; this food is commensurate with his own self, and thus he places this food within him. Or rather...
Food that is commensurate with one's own size protects one and does not harm; that which is more harms, and that which is less does not protect.
They are made of udumbara wood.
The Udumbara is indeed strength and sap; he thus bestows strength and sap upon him. Furthermore, since the Udumbara is all these trees, by laying these down, he lays down all the trees.
At the level of the two Retahsic bricks—heaven and earth are indeed the two Retahsic—he thus places the trees within those two.
Therefore, for these two, the wooden vessels have four corners; for there are four quarters, and thus he places the wooden vessels in all the quarters.
Therefore, there are wooden vessels in all the quarters. In the middle, it is contracted, for the sake of the form of the mortar. 7.5.1. [16]
Furthermore, as to why he places the mortar and pestle:

when Prajāpati had become relaxed, his vital breath (prāṇa) sought to depart from the middle; he held it fast with food (anna). Therefore, the vital breath is held by food; for whoever eats food, he [is one whose breath is held].
It breathes.
When the vital breath was seized, food sought to depart from him; he grasped it with the vital breath. Therefore, food is grasped by means of the vital breath;
for whoever breathes, he eats food.
When both of these had been taken, Vitality (ūrj) sought to depart from him; he seized it with both of these. Therefore, Vitality is taken by means of both of these.
For whoever eats food, breathes, and that [food] gives him strength. 7.5.1. [19]
When *ūrj* (vital energy) was seized, these two desired to go away from him. He seized them with *ūrj*; therefore, both of these [breath and food] exist through *ūrj*.
For whoever gains *ūrj*, he breathes; he eats food. 7.5.1. [20]
These [elements], having been grasped by one another, entered into the Self; and as this food was being entered, all the gods entered after it, for everything here has food as its life. 7.5.1.21.
Regarding this, the following verse is proclaimed:
"He indeed became that vital breath (prāṇa). For he indeed became that vital breath;
"having become great, he became Prajāpati," for he indeed became great when these gods entered him as his enjoyers.
"Having found the servants"—the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) are indeed the "servants" (*bhuj*), and food is the "service" (*bhujiṣyā*); thus, "having found all this.
"Having filled the city"—the self (*ātman*) is indeed the "city" (*pūr*), for it fills; since he filled the vital breaths, therefore the vital breaths are the gods.
And because Prajāpati filled them, therefore Prajāpati is the vital breath. That which is the vital breath is this very Gāyatrī. Now...

That which was the food is this Viṣṇu, the deity; and that which was the *arga* is this *udumbara* tree. He said, "Verily, this has lifted me up from all evil," because he said, "It has lifted me up (*udabharat*)," therefore it is called *udumbara*; for indeed, the *udumbara* is so named because it has lifted him up.

Thus they speak cryptically, for the gods love the cryptic; "May he make wide space for me"—therefore it is called *urukara*. They call it *ulūkhala* cryptically, for the gods love the cryptic. This mortar is the womb of all the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), for the head is indeed [the source] of the vital breaths.
The womb (yoni) is 7.5.1.[23].
It is a span in measure;
for the head is, as it were, a span in measure and is four-cornered.
For the head, as it were, is gathered at its four corners; indeed, the head is as if gathered together in the middle. 7.5.1 [24] When the gods restored him, they placed all this within his middle.
"In this manner, he bestows upon him breath, food, and vigor; with the *retaḥsic* bricks, he places them in the region of the *retaḥsic*s.
The *retaḥsic*s are indeed the ribs, and the ribs are the middle; thus, from the very middle, he bestows all this upon him. 'Behold the deeds of Viṣṇu'."

"Vigour indeed is the work of Viṣṇu; behold his vigours"—this refers to the fact that "he has observed the vows"; for the vow is food, thus it means "from which he has made food visible. "The worthy friend of Indra"—for he is indeed the worthy friend of Indra. He places [the mortar and pestle] with a brick dedicated to two deities, for the mortar and pestle belong to two deities.

He settles it once; he thus makes it uniform, for this food is indeed uniform. Having settled it, he consecrates it with the *sūdadohas* verse; the significance of that has been explained. 7.5.1. [26] Then he lays down the fire-pan (*ukhā*). The fire-pan is indeed the womb; it is thus the womb that he lays down. Upon it [he places] the mortar...

He places [the mortar]. The mortar is indeed the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*). Whatever is above it is the intermediate space; the intermediate space is the middle. Thus he places the womb in the middle. Therefore, the womb of all beings, even of the trees, is in the middle. 7.5.1 [27]
Furthermore, as to why he lays down the fire-pan (ukhā):
Prajāpati, indeed, was that one who fell apart; this fire-pan is those very worlds, for these worlds are Prajāpati. He lays it down upon the mortar (ulūkhala).
Thus he establishes him in all this— in the vital breath, in food, and in strength— and furthermore, he places him so that he is not separated from all this. Then, having ground the *upaśaya* [clay].
Having made the mouth of the *lokabhāj* [the fire-pan] face forward, he pours [the grain] into the pan;
for this indeed is its place, and thus it remains unseparated from it.
Regarding this they say: "How does this [grain] become cooked and placed within the boiled milk?"—by the very fact that it has been consecrated with a *yajus* formula, and furthermore...
Whatever indeed one approaches this Vaiśvānara fire, that very thing becomes cooked, prepared, and offered.
7.5.1 [30] "Thou art firm, a supporter," he says.

Its kinship has been declared; "From here he was born, first from these wombs, Jātavedas"—for indeed, from these wombs Jātavedas was first born. "May he, knowing, carry the oblation to the gods by means of the Gāyatrī, the Triṣṭubh, and the Anuṣṭubh"—by these, indeed, is he [the fire].
Knowing [the way], he carries the oblation to the gods by means of the meters.
"For food, for wealth, rejoice! For power, for splendor, for vigor, for offspring"—for all this.
"Rejoice!"—this means "thou art a sovereign ruler (samrāj), thou art a self-ruler (svarāj)," for he is indeed both a sovereign ruler and a self-ruler.
"May the two Sarasvatī springs come to thee"—Sarasvant is the mind and Sarasvatī is speech; these are the two Sarasvatī springs.
"May they protect thee"—this is what it means. He lays them down with two verses; the significance of this has been explained, for this form consists of a pair.
Having set down the clay and the water, he consecrates it with the *sūdadohas* verse; the significance of this has already been explained.
Then he makes an offering over it.
For indeed, this seed was previously poured into her.

He scatters sand; he thus performs this [act] upon it, and therefore the seed, once poured into the womb, is performed upon. He offers with clarified butter, using a dipping-spoon (*sruva*), with the utterance of *svāhā*, and with two *gāyatrī* verses addressed to Agni; the significance of that has already been explained. "O Agni, yoke those which are thine... (RV 6.16.43) ...[and so forth].
With the two verses beginning "Harness, for you are the best invokers of the gods," he thus harnesses this very seed in the womb; therefore, the seed, once harnessed in the womb, does not flow out.

If it has been maintained for a year, then he should offer the oblation; for that which is maintained for a year is everything, and that which he offers is everything. But if it has not been maintained for a year, he should merely stand near it; for that which is not maintained for a year is not everything.
Now, that which has not been carried for a year is incomplete; therefore, when he performs the *upasthāna* (homage), he should rather offer oblations directly. This Agni is an animal;
he is here prepared whole and complete, and his downward breath is the *svayamātṛṇā* brick.
The two hips are the Dviyajus; the ribs are the two Retahsic bricks; the backbones are the Viśvajyotis; the hump is the Ṛtavyā bricks; the neck is the Aṣāḍhā; the head is the tortoise.

Those vital breaths which are in the tortoise and those vital breaths which are in the head—those are yours. Verily, one builds this very [altar] from here upwards, facing eastward. This Agni is indeed yonder sun; thus, one builds that sun from here.
He places it facing upwards and towards the east; therefore, yonder sun is placed here facing upwards and towards the east. Then he turns it to the right;
he thereby causes yonder sun to turn to the right; therefore, yonder sun—
