The belly is the lower part, and the womb is the female organ; the penis is the pestle, for it is as if circular, since the penis is indeed circular.

He places it on the right side, for the male lies on the right side of the female. That which is the food of the prepared animal is the *dūrveṣṭakā* brick; indeed, its upper half becomes more elevated.
This Agni is an animal; therefore, the upper belly of a well-fed animal becomes more prominent.
He lays down the heads of animals;
the heads of animals are indeed cattle; it is thus cattle that he lays down.
He places them upon the fire-pan (ukhā). The fire-pan is indeed these worlds, and the animal heads are cattle;
he thus places cattle in these worlds, and therefore cattle exist in these worlds. Furthermore, as for [placing them] in the fire-pan:
The fire-pan (ukhā) is indeed the womb, and the heads of the victims are cattle; he thus establishes the cattle in the womb.
Therefore, even though they are being eaten and cooked, cattle are not exhausted, for he establishes them in the womb. Furthermore, as to why he lays down the heads of the victims.
Those splendors are indeed these heads of the sacrificial animals;
and those trunks are these five layers. Those five layers are these worlds;
and since these worlds are this fire-pan (ukhā), when he places the heads of the animals in the fire-pan, he thereby [places] these very heads with these [worlds].
He joins the baskets together.
He places them in front, facing westward.
This is indeed where Prajāpati desired to seize those animals.

Desiring to take possession [of them], they sought to depart; he gathered them together within the vital breaths (*prāṇa*). Having gathered them together within the vital breaths, he placed them within himself from the front toward the back.
That very thing is performed here.
"Whatever the gods did, this [is why] these cattle do not wish to depart from us.
But when he does this, thinking, 'I shall do what the gods did,' he thereby seizes them by their vital breaths and places them within himself from the front toward the back. 7.5.2. [6]
Furthermore, as to why he lays down the heads of the sacrificial animals:
In the beginning, Prajāpati was indeed this universe alone. He desired, "May I create food; may I procreate. From his vital breaths (*prāṇa*) alone, he fashioned out the animals, from his mind.

From his eye he fashioned the horse, from his breath the cow, from his ear the sheep, and from his speech the goat. Because he fashioned these out from his vital breaths (*prāṇa*), they say, "Animals are the vital breaths. Mind is indeed the first of the vital breaths;
because he fashioned man out from mind, they say, "Man is the first of animals."

"The most vigorous one": the mind, indeed, is all the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), for in the mind all the vital breaths are established. Because he fashioned the person (*puruṣa*) from the mind, therefore they say, "The person is all the cattle," for all these belong to the person alone. 7.5.2. [7]

Having created this food, he placed it within his own self from the front; therefore, whoever creates food places it within his own self from the front. That [food] was indeed in the fire-pan (*ukhā*); for the fire-pan is the belly, and that food was in the belly.
He places [the butter]. 7.5.2.[8] Then he throws pieces of gold into these [carts].
Gold, indeed, is breath; and now, from these animals...
The vital breaths depart from those very beings while they are being consoled; therefore, when he throws down pieces of gold, he thereby places the vital breaths back into them.
He throws down seven.

There are indeed seven vital breaths in the head; he thus places them in this [altar]. Now, if there should be five animals, he should throw [the bricks] on each one seven times, five by five. For he lays down these five animals, and in each single animal there are seven vital breaths; thus he places the vital breaths in all of them. 7.5.2. [10]

Regarding this, some indeed do so even when there is only one animal: they throw [the bricks] seven times each, five times over; for he places these five animals, and in each single animal there are seven vital breaths; thus, in all of them—
"One should not do so thinking, 'I am placing the vital breaths [into it],' for in this animal indeed is the form of all animals.
When he pours [the ointment] into this one, he thereby places the vital breaths into all of them. 7.5.2.
He first pours it into the mouth.

"The streams flow together like milch-cows"—for *dhenā* is indeed food; thus this [food] flows together toward the mouth. "Purified within by the heart and the mind"—for within, by means of the heart and the mind, the food that exists is purified. "I behold the streams of that clarified butter belonging to the upright one"—those which...
When he is about to offer oblations into this fire, he says this: "The golden reed is in the midst of the fire.
By this, he refers to that very golden person.
[He says: "For the Ṛc!"—thus here.

The *ṛc* is indeed breath, for by means of breath one praises. "For radiance (*ruk*)"—here, radiance is breath, for by means of breath one shines; moreover, everything here shines for the sake of breath. "For brilliance (*bhās*)"—here; "for light (*jyotis*)"—here;
for these two eyes are brilliant and luminous. "This has become the vigor of the entire world, of Agni Vaiśvānara."

"Here Agni is with light, luminous; the gold plate is with splendor, splendid"—thus [he says] with two verses containing the word "all," for the ear is indeed all-encompassing. 7.5.2. [13] Then he lifts up the human head.
"Thou art a giver of a thousand; for a thousand thee!"—a thousand is indeed everything; thus he means, "Thou art the giver of all; for all thee!
7.5.2.[14] Then he lays them down.
Having reached the first man with his own vigor, he places him in the middle;
he places the other animals on both sides of the man. Thus, he places the eater in the midst of the animals;
therefore, the man alone is the eater in the midst of the animals. 7.5.2. [15]
The horse and the sheep he places to the north; he thus establishes these two animals in that direction, and therefore these two animals are most numerous in that direction. 7.5.2. [16]
The cow and the goat on the south; he places these two animals in that direction, and therefore these two animals are most numerous in that direction. 7.5.2. [17]
He places a man in the milk.
Milk, indeed, is cattle; he thus establishes the sacrificer among cattle.
"Anoint the solar embryo with milk"—for this embryo is indeed the sun.
"When one says, 'Anoint that man with milk,' it means: 'The thousandfold image, the multiformed. Man indeed is the image of the thousandfold, for man becomes a thousandfold.
When one says, 'Avoid him with your heat; do not strike him,' it means: 'Avoid him with your flame; do not harm him; make him long-lived.'"
"In being built up"—this makes the man one whose life among animals lasts for a hundred years; therefore, it is the man alone who has a life of a hundred years among animals. 7.5.2.
[18] Then, on the north side, [he places] the horse with [the verse], "The speed of the wind. For the horse is indeed the speed of the wind. "The navel of Varuṇa"—so [it says].
"For Varuṇa’s horse has been born in the midst of the flood (*sarira*). Now, the flood is indeed the waters, and the horse is born from the waters;

"the tawny infant of the rivers, whose foundation is the pressing-stones. The pressing-stone is indeed a mountain, and the waters have mountains as their foundation. "O Agni, do not harm him in the highest heaven!"—these worlds are indeed the highest heaven; thus he means, "do not harm him in these worlds. (7.5.2)
Then, on the south side, [he addresses] the cow with the verse, "The unceasing, ruddy drop" (*ajasram indum aruṣam*). The drop (*indu*) is indeed Soma; this cow is that very Soma which is unceasing.
"The supporter" (*bhuraṇyu*) means "the sustainer. With the words, "I praise Agni, the first-thinker, with prostrations" (*agnim īḷe pūrvacittim namobhiḥ*), it is indeed related to Agni.
"The cow has recognized the ancient thought"—for they carry the fire forward and attend to it facing forward.
"He who is being fashioned according to his joints and seasons"—for when this [fire-altar] is built, then it is indeed fashioned by its joints according to the seasons.
"Do not harm the cow, the Aditi, the Virāj"—the cow is indeed the Virāj, and the Virāj is food; the cow is food. 7.5.2. [20]
Then, on the north side, [he lays down] the ewe with [the verse], "The guardian of Varuṇa, the navel of Tvaṣṭṛ. For this ewe belongs both to Varuṇa and to Tvaṣṭṛ;
[with the words] "Born from the highest realm," the highest realm is indeed the ear, for the quarters are the ear, the highest realm.

"O Earth, the thousandfold illusion of the Asura"—this means "the great, thousandfold illusion of the Asura. "O Agni, do not harm him in the highest heaven"—the highest heaven is indeed these worlds; thus, it means "do not harm him in these worlds. 7.5.2. [21]
Then, on the south side, [he places] the goat with [the verse],
"The fire which was born from Agni"— for this fire was indeed born from Agni;
"from the heat of the earth or from the sky"— for that which was born from Prajāpati’s heat was born from both the sky and the earth.
And from grief was born the goat (*aja*), by whom Viśvakarman produced offspring; for the goat is indeed speech, and through speech Viśvakarman produced offspring.
"O Agni, let thy wrath pass him by"—as the sacrificial formula is, so is its significance.
These, then, are the animals.
He piles them separately, settles them separately, and pronounces the *sūdadohas* verse over them separately, for these animals are distinct. Then he offers an oblation upon the head of the man.
The oblation is indeed the sacrifice; it thereby makes the person worthy of sacrifice among animals.
Therefore, the person alone sacrifices among animals. Furthermore, as for why he offers this oblation over it:

He places that vigor in the head; he offers with clarified butter, for clarified butter is a thunderbolt and the thunderbolt is indeed vigor; thus he bestows vigor upon him. With the utterance of *svāhā*, for the *svāhā*-utterance is a bull and the bull is indeed vigor; thus he bestows vigor upon him. With a *triṣṭubh* verse, for the *triṣṭubh* is a thunderbolt and the thunderbolt is indeed vigor.
The *triṣṭubh* is vigor; by means of vigor he thus bestows vigor upon him.
He recites a half-verse and utters "svāhā.
For the *ṛc* is bone; having thus separated this skull-bone from it.
Whatever vigor is within the head, that he places therein.
Then, having recited the subsequent half-verse, he utters "svāhā," thereby joining together this skull-bone of the head.
"That which is the vigor above the head, that he places in this [brick].
"The bright face of the gods has risen up"—
this person here is indeed yonder sun, and that is the bright one.

"The host of the gods rises—the eye of Mitra, Varuṇa, and Agni"—for this is indeed the eye of both the gods and men. "He has filled heaven, earth, and the intermediate space"—for as he rises, he fills these worlds. "Sūrya is the soul of all that moves and stands"—for he is indeed the soul of all this, and whatever there is.
"And the world that stands. 7.5.2.[28] Then he worships with the *utsarga* formulas. Indeed, when Prajāpati desired to obtain these animals, they, being about to be obtained—
They grieved; by these offerings they cast away their grief and their evil.
In the same way, this [sacrificer] now, by these offerings, casts away his grief and his evil.
Now, some indeed place whichever animal it may be upon the altar.

They cast off the impurity of that [brick], thinking, "Lest we should lay down impurity and evil. Yet they do indeed lay down impurity and evil; for whatever impurity they cast off from the preceding one, they lay it down together with the succeeding one. 7.5.2. [30]
Some, however, worship while walking around;
[thinking], "We cast off our heat upwards. They indeed follow after their heat and evil, for by this rite one goes upwards; thus they cast off their heat upwards. 7.5.2. [31]
He should cast the fire outside;

for this fire is these worlds, so he places the affliction outside of those worlds. Outside the altar; for this altar is this [earth], so he places the affliction outside of it. Standing facing north, on this [earth]...
These two directions are the animals; thus, wherever these animals are, there he places this vital sap (ūcu) into them. 7.5.2.
[32] He releases the man first, for he lays him down first. "This me... (he says).

"Do not harm the two-footed beast"—for this man is indeed a two-footed beast; "do not harm him," so it means. "Thousand-eyed, being piled for the sacrifice"—for he is thousand-eyed by means of the gold chips;
"for the sacrifice," that is, "for food. "O Agni, enjoy the Mayu beast as the sacrificial offering"—the *kimpuruṣa* is indeed the Mayu.

"O Agni, accept the Mayu as a Kimpuruṣa"—by this he means, "Building up your bodies, settle down. The body is indeed the self; thus, "building up [yourself], perfect your self. "Let your heat reach the Mayu, let your heat reach him whom we hate"—thereby he places the heat both upon the Mayu and upon him whom he hates. 7.5.2. [33]
Then for the horse:

"Do not harm this one-hoofed animal"—for this horse is indeed a one-hoofed animal; thus he means, "do not harm him. "The loudly neighing, prize-winning steed among prizes"—for this horse is indeed a loudly neighing, prize-winning steed among prizes.
"I assign to you the wild ox," he says; thus he assigns the wild ox to him.
"Building with it, may you settle your bodies," he says; this means, "Building with it, perfect yourself.
"May its heat reach the ox, and may its heat reach him whom we hate," he says; thus he places the heat in the ox and in him whom he hates. 7.5.2. [34]
Now, regarding the cow: "This thousandfold, hundred-streamed well," for this cow is indeed a thousandfold, hundred-streamed well;

"in the midst of the moving flood," for these worlds are the flood, and she is being made to yield sustenance within these worlds; "milking Aditi for the people, yielding ghee," for she, as Aditi, milks ghee for the people; "O Agni, do not... [the verse continues].

"Do not harm him in the highest heaven"—the highest heaven is indeed these worlds; thus he says, "Do not harm him in these worlds. "I assign to you the wild gavaya"—he thereby assigns the wild gavaya to him.
"Building with it, settle your bodies"—"building with it, perfect yourself," this is what he means. "The gavaya is yours..."
"Let heat reach him whom we hate; let your heat reach him," he says; thus he places heat in the gayal and in him whom he hates.
7.5.2. [35] Now, regarding the sheep: "This woolly one"—that is, "this one possessing wool"—"the navel of Varuna," for the sheep belongs to Varuna; [he lays down] a skin.

"Of beasts, both bipeds and quadrupeds"—this is indeed the skin of both kinds of beasts, bipeds and quadrupeds. "'The first birthplace of Tvaṣṭṛ’s offspring'—for it was Tvaṣṭṛ who first fashioned this form. "'O Agni, do not harm [us] in the highest heaven!'—the highest heaven is indeed these worlds; [do not harm us] in them."

"Do not harm him in the worlds"—this he says. "I assign to you the wild camel," by this he assigns the wild camel to him. "Building with it, may you settle your bodies"—by this he means, "Building with it, perfect yourself. "May its heat reach the camel, and may its heat reach him whom we hate"—thus he [assigns it] both to the camel and [to the enemy].
He brings grief upon himself and upon him whom he hates.

7.5.2.[36] Now, regarding the goat: "The goat was born from Agni’s heat (*śoka*). For that which was born from Prajāpati’s heat was indeed born from Agni’s heat. "He, the progenitor, beheld the Father first. Prajāpati is indeed the progenitor; he beheld Prajāpati first.

"By this, the gods attained divinity in the beginning"—the goat is indeed speech; by means of speech, the gods attained divinity in the beginning. "By this, the worthy ones ascended the ascent"—the ascent is indeed the heavenly world;
by this they ascended to the heavenly world, [saying] "the worthy ones. "I grant you the forest deer"—this he gives to him.

"He points out the Śarabha of the forest; piling with it, may he sit down for his own bodies"—this means "piling with it, prepare yourself. "May your heat reach the Śarabha, may your heat reach him whom we hate"—thereby he places the heat both in the Śarabha and in him whom he hates. 7.5.2. [37]

Regarding this they say: "That impurity and evil which Prajāpati drove away from these animals became these five animals; they have departed from the essence of sacrifice (*utkrānta-medhas*), they are impure and unfit for sacrifice. A Brāhmaṇa should not eat of them. He places them in this direction; therefore, in this direction Parjanya does not rain where these [animals] are."
[The verses] are as follows: 7.5.2.[38] Having returned, he worships the fire-altar.
For he acts improperly when [the altar] has been only half-built in the fire.
"Outside the sacrificial altar"—he thus conceals this from him for the sake of non-injury; with a verse addressed to Agni, he conceals this from Agni himself;
with a Gāyatrī verse, for Agni is of the Gāyatrī metre; as great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, by just that much he conceals this from him;
with an undefined verse—for the undefined is everything—he thus conceals this from him by means of everything; and with a verse containing the word "youngest," for that is his beloved abode.

"O youngest one" (yaviṣṭha): because as soon as he was born, he took possession of all this, therefore he is the youngest. "O youngest one, protect the giver"—the sacrificer is indeed the giver; "protect the men"—human beings are indeed "men" (naraḥ).
"Listen to our song"—that is, "listen to this hymn of praise. "Protect our offspring and yourself"—for offspring are indeed *toka*;
thus it means, "protect both the offspring and yourself.
Having climbed onto the fire-altar and gone around behind the *svayamātṛṇṇā* brick, he lays down the *apasyā* bricks.
These are the waters, for they are the *apasyās*;
moreover, the waters have indeed departed from these animals.
Therefore, when he lays down the *apasyās*, he places the waters in these very animals, so that they are not separated from the animals.
He places them so as not to be separated; thus he bestows water upon the cattle. He places them five by five, for these cattle are fivefold.
He places them on all sides; thus he bestows water upon them from every side.
Now, those which are the fifteen preceding ones—

Those [waters] are the active ones; the waters are indeed the thunderbolt, and the thunderbolt is the fifteenfold [stoma]. Therefore, wherever the waters flow, they strike away evil there. Indeed, the thunderbolt strikes away the evil of that region.
Therefore, when it rains, one should walk about uncovered, thinking, "May this thunderbolt of mine strike away evil. 7.5.2. [42]
Now, as for those [bricks] that are five more:

they are the *candas* (metres). The metres are indeed cattle, and cattle are food; and the flesh of cattle is food. Now, it is from these cattle that the various meats have departed; therefore, they are the *candas*.

He places them; he thus places flesh within these very animals. He places them so as not to be separated from the animals; he thus places flesh so as not to be separated from the animals. The *apasyā* bricks are inside and the *candasyā* bricks are outside, for water is inside and flesh is outside. 7.5.2 [43]

Regarding this they say: "If these are the waters and these are the meats, then where is the skin and where are the hairs? Food, indeed, is the skin of the animal, and food is the hair. Now, when he lays down the *candasyā* bricks, that is the skin of the animal and that is its hair.
Furthermore, those hairless pieces which are in the fire-pan (*ukhā*) are the hairs; the fire-pan is on the outside and the heads of the animals are on the inside.
"For the outer hair is the inner self; whether by the one or by the other," so said Śāṇḍilya, "we thus consecrate all the animals in their entirety.
Furthermore, as to why he lays down the Apasyā bricks.
From Prajāpati, when he was relaxed, the waters flowed forth; when they had flowed forth, he entered them. Because he entered them, there are twenty [fingers]. They flowed from his fingers;
for the fingers are the extremities, and it was from the extremities that those waters flowed forth from him. 7.5.2. [45]
He who was that Prajāpati who fell apart is this very Agni who is now being built up; and those waters which flowed away from him are these very Apasyā bricks.
Thus, when he lays down these bricks, it is those very waters which flowed away from him that he restores.
He places this upon this; therefore he lays these down here.
"I settle thee in the lap of the waters," he says.
Vāyu is indeed the lap of the waters, for when he blows hither and thither, then the waters [flow].
They go into the wind; he deposits it with, "I deposit thee in the swelling of the waters.
The swelling of the waters is indeed the plants, for wherever the waters moisten, there they remain.
"Then the plants are born. He places it among the plants.
(7.5.2.48) "I place you in the ashes of the waters," he says; for the cloud is indeed the ash of the waters; he thus places it in the cloud. (7.5.2.49)
"I set thee in the light of the waters," he says;
for lightning is indeed the light of the waters; he thus sets it in the lightning.
"I set thee in the path of the waters," he says.
This earth, indeed, is the place of rest for the waters, for in it the waters go; he settles it there.
Thus, those waters which flowed away from these forms of his, he now restores to him; and moreover, he thereby bestows these very forms upon him. 7.5.2. [51]
"In the ocean, in the seat, I settle you"—the ocean is indeed the vital breath; he settles it in the vital breath. "In the sea, in the seat, I settle you."
The mind, indeed, is the ocean. From the ocean of the mind, with speech as a shovel, the gods dug out the threefold knowledge. Regarding this, there is this verse recited:
"The gods who dug out the ocean with sharp shovels—may the virtuous man know today that place where [they found it]."

“They have offered the oblation,” he says; the mind is the ocean, speech is the sharp axe, and the threefold knowledge is the oblation—this very verse is recited, and he places it within the mind. “I place thee in the body, in the seat,” he says.
Speech, indeed, is the body; he settles it in speech.
"I settle thee in the abode of the waters," he says.
The eye, indeed, is the abode of the waters, for in it the waters always dwell.
He places it in the eye with [the formula]:
"I place thee in the seat of the waters. Now, the seat of the waters is indeed the ear; he thus places it in the ear. That which...
From these forms of his, the waters departed; he now restores them to him, and thus he places those very forms within him. "I set thee in the seat of the waters," [he says].

"The sky is indeed the seat of the waters, for the waters are seated in the sky; he settles her in the sky. "I settle thee in the gathering-place of the waters"—the atmosphere is indeed the gathering-place of the waters; he settles her in the atmosphere.
"In the womb of the waters I settle thee," he says;
for the ocean is indeed the womb of the waters; in the ocean he settles it.
"In the soil of the waters I settle thee," he says.
Sand is indeed the sediment of water; he places it upon the sand with the formula, "I place thee in the domain of the waters.
The domain of the waters is food; he thus places it in food. That which...
From these forms the waters came forth; he now restores them to him, and moreover, he bestows these very forms upon him. "With the Gāyatrī metre I settle thee."

"With the *traiṣṭubha* metre I settle you; with the *jāgata* metre I settle you; with the *ānuṣṭubha* metre I settle you; with the *pāṅkta* metre I settle you"—thereby he restores to him those waters which flowed away from these metres; and furthermore...
He places these very *candāṃsi* in him; these are the fingers. These [are they]. 7.5.2. [62]
He lays them down on all sides, for these fingers are on all sides;
he lays them down at the ends, for these fingers are at the ends; he lays them down in fourfold fashion, for these fingers are fourfold;
he lays them down five by five, for these fingers are five by five; he lays them down separately, for these [fingers] are separate.
He places the fingers down one by one; he makes them equal, therefore they have a common connection.
